We had the pleasure, a few days since of examining a piece of the Atlantic Telegraph Cable, brought hither by Captain Sabroe, of the Packet Schooner Rosaline, to whom it has been kindly lent by a gentleman in St. Thomas. The piece is about three inches long ; and consists of a strand of seven copper wires, enclosed first within a thick coating of gutta-percha, to insulate it from all conducting influences ; and then in a layer of ropeyarn, saturated with a compound of tar and oil. The copper core, gutta-percha sheath, and hempen greatcoat, are next all enveloped together in an investment of iron wire, bound closely round them to furnish tenacity and strength. The Cable is altogether about eleven-sixteenths of an inch thick. It is an error to suppose, as some do, that around the iron wires a thick coating of gutta-percha is again placed. The Cable was laid in the same condition as the piece we examined, and no fears are entertained for the copper wires, should even the iron coating be corroded away. It is however asserted by practical men, that the fine iron used in the wire is not effected by sea water, .as larger masses of coarser iron, such as anchors, are. It is rather expected that a calcareous deposit will be formed around it and thus cement it firmly to the bottom. The piece of the Cable to which we allude may now be 'seen at the Agency of the St. Thomas Bank.

The redoubtable "Old þÿCharley has addressed a letter to the public press, in which he refutes Mr. þÿLindsay depreciation s of the French navy. He argues sensibly and temperately for an increase of our naval strength, and such a state of preparation as should guard us against surprise. He says : þÿ "We must either arrange with France to keep up a moderate navy, or we must keep up a well manned and well-disciplined Channel fleet ; and this may be done at a very moderate expense. At last we have a Channel squadron of six sail of the line, but that is not sufficient ; we ought to have 10 sail of the line, manned by first-rate seamen þÿ there ought not to be a landsman among them. Only 100 marines should be embarked in each ship, and their number filled up with able seamen. Our marines should be increased 5,000 men (which I see wo are about to do), and all our seaport towns garrisoned by them. This I pointed out years ago. We ought always to have 10 sail of the line in reserve and ready, so that in the event of war, or armament, the Channel fleet should turn over one watch to the reserve, fill both up with officers, marines and boys, call out the coast volunteers for landsmen, and wc should have 20 sail of the line better manned than the generality of our ships last war. That is not all ; wc have, or shall soon have, 10,000 Coast-guardsmen. They are for the protection of the revenue, and must not be disturbed unless in case of emergency. They are all told off and ready

to be put on board a ship ; but wc have no ships to receive them, for I do not call the bluckships fit for that purpose. Three of them are tolerable, but the rest are worse than useless. As soon as we have efficient ships ready

Thus would be ready to put to with at any moment 30 sail of the line. And sea such a force at the beginning of a war we could defy the world. There was no manoeuvring, and we were not on board of any nut the flag-ship, and therefore could not judge either of their discipline or crews. 1 went with Mr. Linds ly on board the Bretagne, and 1 agree with him, she is a magnificent ship. There was no preparation for us ; quite the contrary, the men were at their bags, dressing to receive the Queen, but everything seemed in the highest order, and the ship was beautifully fitted. Indeed, all French ships arc ; they arc all alike, and everything in its place. Whether the men were sailors or not I cannot say, but they appeared to me to be strong, healthy men. Mr. Lindsay compares the Royal Albert with the Bretagne, and ho says, if both were manned with Frenchmen, the Royal Albert would sink the Bretagne ; but he þÿdon tell t us why. The Bretagne is a much larger ship, and mounts more guns, and has more men ; therefore it ought to be quite the other way. Were the Royal Albert to meet

The year 1»6S will form a marked period in history for the extraordinary impetus given to J the extension of settlement and to Commercial activity in the northern countries ou the Asia T: and American sides of the Pacific. The Russians, who have loDg been seeking an ocean Port lor their Commerce and ships, have of late years been pursuing with great perseverance their extension policy in Manchooria, and, as we have already stated, have managed to share very successfully in the diplomatic arrangements brought about by the recent combined proceedings in the Gulf of Peieliow. They had already taken possession of the Anioor River, occupied its hanks, colonised it, and covered its waters with steamers, aud the recent Russian despatch announces that a special treaty gives, among other things, possession of the left bank of the river to them. Stray uotiees have front time to time appeared of the movements of the Russians in that far distant region, hut the British public generally have very little conception of the strides they have made, in that quarter Not that we can object to their colonising and improving the district, if it he fit lor the purpose, for we would rather meet the Russians in the friendly contest of Commerce than in the more stern and fatal combat of war Russian policy has already reclaimed and utilised vast tracts of that enormous stretch ol couutry over which the Government holds sway, aud the present ruler will no doubt push civilisation, Commerce, and the scientific

improvements of the day into many of the waste places of Siberia, and parts of Central Asia. It appears from reliable accounts that there are now no less than twenty-nine steam-boats ou the waters of the Amoor River, fourteen of which are Russian war steamers, and the remainder private steamers belonging to Russians and Americans. Nicolayefsky, the town formed at the mouth of the Ainoor. is rising into considerable importance. It has been made a free þÿI ort in order to attract Commerce. Foreign Merchants and settlers are presented with allotments of ground for their warehouses free of any rent or charge whatever, assisted in their avocations and business in the most liberal way, exempted from taxation, and are even afforded Help to clear the ground and erect their houses. Hence many Gormans, Americans, and others have set. tied on the Amoor, looking to the extension of

Commerce aud business iu the supply of stores j to Siberia, aud the trade with the adjoining islands and the European settlements in North- Western America. A Russian Company has also, we find, been formed for developing the resources of the Amoor district, which proposes to trado with the people of the surrounding districts, bartering with them goods for skius and other indigenous products The supply of the wauts of the Russian Colonists, now becoming numerous on the banks of the Amoor, is a main object, as well as the extension of foreign Commerce with the Ports of the Eastern Ocean, and trade with places iu the iuterior. The prosecution of the Fisheries is to be another primary pursuit, and also the whaling trade in the Eastern Ocean and the adjacent waters, it is also proposed to maintain steamers aud sailing-vessels on the coast aud on the Amoor and tshilk Rivers, to form manufactories and working establishments of different kinds, and to take G ivernim nt and private contracts in Eastern Siberia and the Amoor country- The importance of the River Amoor to Russia, as a direct line of communication between her Asiatic territories and the Pacific, is very great. Navigable for nearly 1,400 miles, it has speedily become the great line of import aud export for Asiatic Russia. When we find that the Government of Russia can communicate already, under existing arrangements aud disadvantages, with the distant impetus will be giveu portion of its territory iu when a month, a surprising the telegraph line

proposed several years ago, and doubtless now in course of formation, is completed. This line was to run from Moscow, across the Ural Mountains into Asia, passing through Irkutsk, the capital of Eastern Siberia, to tno Sea of Okhotsk, and tlicucc across the Sra ol Rauitschatka to þÿCook s lexicographical canon declares that a dic- Inlet, in Russian America. This line would also connect with the Amoor River aud Monehooria. We mention prominently these facts of Russian progress in order to infuse some energy into our own proceedings with regard to British Columbia and Vancouver. Let us at least have a Commercial Port and Naval Station on t ho Pacific of equal importance to Russia. Let us promote, rather than discourage, bona fide settlement in the North-West, make the Port of þÿVancouver Island s also a free Port, and enact taxi s of the lightest possible character. With the transference of the larger portion of the Chinese trade to the more important northern districts, aud the opening of trado with the rivers and great inteii >r, a British settlement in the north is of the utmost importance ; and for sueh pur-
poses as a depot and harbour ot refit, .V'' , Hong Kong, in the -outh, will be utterly useless.

The sound of rejoicing for the completion of the tel graphic communication between England and America had hardly ceased on both sides (if the ocean which lias been so wonderfully intersected by the wire, and the ovations and festivities in honour of those who were intrumental in achieving the great work were still nt their height at this side of the Channel, when a gloom was cast upon all by the sudden and unexpected announcement that intelligible signals had ceased to come through the success The public and those interested in the cable. of the undertaking have, doubtless, been much surprised to that so many allowed elapse since the announcement of days should have been the failure of signals without their being acquainted, either through of the the company or newspaper correspondence, progress of affairs at this terminal of the Atlantic wire. But the fact is, that, bey. ml the bare fact that signals were not received, there lias been nothing to communicate until the results of the investigations of Profess r Thomson, Mr. Edward Bright. Mr Vark-y, and other scientific gentlci. n, w' o have been experimenting upon the aide for t ( past few days, had transpired. In order to in ke the present con iition i f the cable per-

fectly understood it will necessary to trace its history from previous to the landing of the end at Valentia down to the present time. In a former communication containing the particulars of the last successful c nise. of the Agamemnon it will be rente nb i that r t ere nee was made to a very sei ct.ical fault having occuried in the cabh on Sunday, August the 1st, after about one-half of the distance | iiom miil-oci an to the shores of Ireland had been traversed. Though that fault ( which was app.ueiitly a Leak in the continuity of the conductor) gradually recovered itself after having caused gr. at trouble and anxiety for question i some 13 hours, yet the electrical condition of the cable had evidently icceived a shock from which it icr completely recovered. This was, however, regarded as a matter of very little consequence, as the currents which were both received and transmitted were sufficiently good for all the purposes of telegraphing. During the remaining three or four days which were occupied in submerging the remainder of the wire its electrical condition was very variable, being at times very good and occasionally indifferent. These variations were at the time referred to the effects of magnetic storms aud earth currents, but at no time was its condition so defective as in any degree to impair the landing telegraphic communication. From the time to the end, on the 5th of August, of condition, Monday, the 9th, the cable continued in conse- though a slight defect, of no fair

quence in working, was observed in the insulation. Up to that evening nothing but alternate positive and negative currents had words ceived from Newfoundland, though been re- and adjustment messages had from soon after the That landing been continually coil sent the words evening, " Send however, slower currents and from Valentia. repeat'' came with from Newfoundland, being sent by Mr. Whitehouse's instruments, aud received upon his beautifully constructed recording relay. It was soon

found, however, that Mr Whitebousu's receiving relay, though admirably adapted for receiving messages through the cable, had been adjusted and constructed under the very natural belief that the cable, if landed at all, would have suffered little in its electrical condition, and it was found not to work with certainty with the comparatively feeble signals which arrived from the American continent. Professor Thomson's delicate reflecting galvanometer was accordingly substituted for it, though messages were transmitted from both ends as usual by Mr. Whitehouse's patent. It is necessary to mention these apparently trifling circumstances, in order to correct an erroneous impression which has doubtless unintentionally been created by a letter recently published by Mr. Whiteliouse. No one cau deny the inestimable services rendered to the cause of Atlantic telegraphy by Mr. Whitchouse in his capacity of electrician, or the energy and perseverance with which be pursued his electrical experiments through a long period, when it was more than doubtful whether the cable would ever be laid to render practical his discoveries and inventions. Whatever may be the merits of the dispute between Mr. Whitehousc and the Atlantic Telegraph Company, whether he has or has not been harshly treated, is a question between him and the directors, with which the public have no concern It is necessary here to enter thus far into the question to correct the impression which Mr. Whitvhouse's

letter no doubt unintentionally conveyed, that his instruments alone were used in the receipt and transmission of all the messages which passed through the Atlantic cable. During the whole of the week, front Monday, the 9th, to Saturday, the 14th, various adjustment messages were received and sent through the line, though, in consequence of their constantly requiring messages from Valentin to 1 rep .ted several times, it was evident that in Nov t .. ndland the signals wore not read with the same facility as those in the contrary direction to Valentin. This circumstance tended to prove that the fault which was observable was somewhere near the Irish coast, for any defect more than 300 miles from either coast would affect the transmission and reception of signals equally at both ends. Accordingly the cable was undcrrun for the distance of about three miles from Valentin Island by Mr. Canning, cut, and tested through by Mr. Bartholomew, the electrical superintendent, who found that whatever fault existed was far out to sea. The ends were accordingly joined up again without a new piece of cable being laid between Dinvlnshead aud the shore. From this to Saturday, the 21st of August, the fault was very variable both in its nature and its apparent distance from the Irish coast, it first appearing something like 500 miles distant, and gradually diminishing until it became stationary at a point calculated with great accuracy to be nearly 270 statute miles from the Valentin end of the

cable. All this period the electrical condition became daily worse and worse, and it was only with the greatest difficulty and by constant repetitions that the various official and congratulatory messages between the English and American authorities were transmitted to Newfoundland, the messages back to Valentin being in almost every case clear and distinct. The condition of the wire became daily more faulty until the 31st of August, when a Government message was despatched through the cable for the North American colonies, and on the morning of the 1st of September a second Government message was safely transmitted, but after it had been duly acknowledged the insulation of the wire became suddenly worse, and it was found impossible to make them understand at Newfoundland. Words and messages were continually transmitted, but it was soon evident that on the American shore they could only just distinguish that signals were being sent, for the only answer received at Valentia was " Repeat'' and " Don't understand," and even these small phrases were only distinguishable at intervals ; and since half-past 1 o'clock on the morning of Friday, the 4th of September, no intelligible signal whatever has been received. Occasionally, however, very distinct reversals (as regularly alternating positive and negative currents are termed) have been received, sometimes so strong and good that had they been sending words from Newfoundland they might have been distinctly read on the reflecting gal-
vanometer of Professor Thomson. When the

CROIX AVIS . line is not in use for the purpose of testing words, short messages are continually despatched through the wire for an hour at a time, and then for the next hour the galvanometer is watched for the answers, which, excepting the reversals already alluded to, never come. From the time of the first cessation of the rignals up to the present time Professor W. Thomson, Mr. Varlcy, and Mr. Edward Bright have been engaged day and night in testing, aud have come to the conclusion that the defect is a loss of insulation about 270 miles (along the cable) from Valentia. This, calculating the amount of slack cable paid out during the later days of the submerging operations, would place the fault about 220 statute miles from shore, or somewhere upon the mountain range which divides the depth of the Atlantic from the comparatively shallow water leading from the Irish coast. Reference to logs and diaries kept by those on hoard the Agamemnon during the submerging operations show that this bank was crossed between 4 and 5 o'clock on the afternoon of the 3d of August, more than an hour before the expected time. It had been intended by Sir Charles Bright to allow a great quantity of slack cable to run out while crossing this point, in order that it might reach the bottom of all the inequalities which might exist there undiscovered by the sounding line. But, from some unexplained cause, the Agamemnou throughout the whole cruise steamed at a greater speed than was registered by the log-line.

Owing to this circumstance the bank was reached at least an hour before the expected time, the first intimation received by those on board being a sudden decrease in the registered strain upon the dynamometer and an equally sudden falling off in the speed of the cable, the ship maintaining the saute rate, as registered by the log-line. Sir Charles Blight's attention was e red to the circumstance, and he, seeing at ouce that the shallow water was approaching, or had actually been reached, ordered the weight to be taken oil' the breaks, and allow a large quantity of slack cable to go overboard. It must always remain a matter of doubt, however, whether the falling off of the strain on and speed of the cable was observable at all until the top of the bank had been reached, and had this been the case it is quite possible that the cable may have remained suspended upon some projecting points in the steep, and its insulation sooner become gradually injured by its own weight. This is, of course, only a probable conjecture, based upon the facts above stated. But at the same time it is impossible to account in any other way for the cable having become damaged since its submersion. Should the fault have originated in this way not the least blame is attributable cither to Sir Charles Bright, his assistants, or the officers of the Agamemnon, the occurrence being solely referable to the defective and uucertain method of ascertaining the speed of a ship at present in vogue in the Royal navy. The steeji range

above alluded to is often mentioned as a sloping bank, upon what ground it is difficult to say, for but two soundings were taken upon it, one tit tiio bottom and another at the top, and these two soundings, though only eight miles apart, show a difference in elevation of 7,200 feet. Of the nature of the interveniug space no one can of course form any conjecture. Whether the sides of this submarine mountain (for it can be called nothing else) are broken by ravines and precipitous cliffs in the same way as the sides of the mountains on land are, nothing but a close and careful series of soundings can ever determine. That such a series of soundings were not made by Commander Dayman at the point in question, when he sounded we across the Atlantic from the Cyclops, was, believe, duo to the prevalence of bad weather at the time. It is perfectly conclusive, according to the experiments of l'rofessor Thomson and Mr. Varley, that the water has reaohed the conducting wire in at least one aud miles from the shore, place not less than 220 as the currents received from Newfoundland vary from one twohundreth to only one uinc-hundreth part of the strength they should be, it would be deceiving the public to state that the fault is other than of the most serious nature. But still it is believed possible by some, with more delicate instruments, and with proper concert at both cuds of the line, to work through during some part of each day, provided the condition of the wire becomes no worse. Negative currents of electricity are now
used as much as possible in the transmission of

signals, for were positive currents used the exposed portion of the wire, by decomposing the salt water in contact with it, would be oxidized through in a very short time. Mr. Ileuley, who has beeu for some days experimenting upon the cable, is sanguine of making the line again serviceable, by the use of his powerful magnetoelectric machines, which are now on their way from Loudon. It is as well that every expedient for working the lino in its present defective condition be tried, as the chances of successfully underrunning the cable as far as the point, of injury arc unfortunately very small indeed The extraordinary phenomena of the natural currents of electricity, which are continually traversing the surface of the earth in various directions, act by their inductive effects upon the great length of cable submerged, aud disturb the needles and galvanometers at both ends of the line to a considerable degree. This nature and action, if properly observed aud studied by means of the Atlantic cable, would, no doubt, throw considerable light upon the phenomena of diurnal magnetic variations, to account for which no satisfactory law has been proposed. On the night of Monday, the 6th of September, one of those extraordinary phenomena called magnetic storms must have passed over the track of the cable, for from half-past 11 to half-past 12 the reflecting galvanometer in connexion with the line was most violently disturbed. The reflections were so rapid and violent that it was only occasionally

that the reflected ray of light could be distinguished upon the reading scale . These magnetic storms are of by no means rare occurrence, and as well as the earth currents already mentioned, sometimes cause great delay and annoyance on long lines of telegraphic communication. There is still a very generally prevalent idea that one of the principal faults in the cable is comparatively near shore, and though this supposition is opposed to the very conclusive experiments of Professor Thomson and Mr \ arley, yet it is a question whether, for the full satisfaction of the shareholders, it would not be worth while taking up the cable for a few miles from cither shore, and then testing through the middle portioi. These operations would undoubtedly be attended with considerable expense, and it is, therefore, probably not thought advisable to engage in them until it has been ascertained how matters stand at the American terminus ol the cable. Mr. Lundy, one of the electrical assistants, proceeds to Newfoundland on Tuesday, by the Prince Albert, from Galway, for the purpose of ascertaining the condition of the wire at the other terminus, and also for the purpose of arranging a day on which a certain new code of signals are to he sent at concerted times from both cuds, and to endeavour thus to re-establish intelligible communication. Even looking the matters in the worst light, and supposing at cable as far as practical working goes a failure, not only has the practicability of submerging it

been demonstrated, but also tbc practicability of working and signalling through it. Therefore, it is not to be supposed for one moment that the i i i public, both on this and the other side of the Atlantic, will ever allow the grand scheme for connecting together the Old and the New World to fall to the ground, even if ten cables instead of one be sacrificed in its accomplishment. At the same time, private enterprise, unless adequately encouraged by the two Governments, cannot bo expected to come forward and expend vast sums of money in the manufacture and submerging of another cable, with a fair chance against them of losing both capital have The Atlantic Telegraph Company and interest. expended nearly half-a-million in the manufacture ami laying of the present cable, for which the English aud American Governments guarantee 28,000/. a-year for a certain period, contingent upon success. But should the present cable prove a failure both the capital and the Government subsidy are lost, and the shareholders are expected to subscribe another half-million for another wire on the self-same basis as before, and with the same chance of losing all before tbein. Under these circumstances it is not surprising the difliculliesof raising the capital for a new cable arc looked upon as almost iusurtnountablo If the English and American Governments are really anxious for an effective telegraphic communication between the two countries, they have but to guarantee -a certain though small percentage on
the total capital expended in the completion of the line, and money will be forthcoming for new wires should five or six be lost before one is successfully completed.

From the London Times, Sept. 17. The Treaty of Tien-sin is one of those facts which will grow larger as time wears on, and will be more conspicuous io the eyes of the next generation than it is in ours. We shall think no space misspent which can be employed in giving to this event its proper importance among the transactions of our age, and in informing the public mind as to its character, and probable results. There arc, doubtless, many circumstances of the antecedent negotiations which cannot now be revealed, and there arc certainly some facts which could not be judiciously made the subject of public comment. We may regret this, for we believe that if we could have the same detailed knowledge of the negotiations at Tien-sin which Bit Torcy has given us of the negotiations of the Treaty of Utrecht, we should be better able to render justice to the firmness and sagacity of Lord Elgin, and to the prompt and intelligent zeal of the Secretary of Legation and members of the Staff. If our information be correct, the two most important articles of tilts Treaty þÿ the Resident Minister at Pekin, and the right of Englishmen to go to any part of the empire for curiosity or trade þÿ were in peril at the very last moment, and were obtained by England singlehanded, and only by a stroke of happy audacity Whenever these stories of baffled intrigues become lawful history they wilt add another illustration to all we already know of Russian diplomacy, and tend to show the had results of keeping doubtful company. When

the Russian and American eagles take a companion flight the younger bird does the work and the elder eats the prey. There is, however, one fact connected with these strangely involved intrigues which is not without its interest. We mentioned some time since that Keying, the negotiator of the Nankin Treaty in 1842, had acted a sort of independent guerrilla part in these negotiations, and having been countermined and exposed had gone hack to Pekin. Wo now hear that the life, of this poor old man has been sacrificed. On his way back to the capital the General commanding at. Tung-cliow arrested him as a deserter from his

post. Two Princes of that mediately memorialized be might be executed. The Emperor ordered him to be tried, and the Court sentenced him to public disgrace and decapitation. Just as the advices left the decree had come down. The Emperor says that ia his mercy he took Keying out of disgrace and sent him to try to soothe the foreigner, believing he knew how to do so. Lo ! the next he hears of him is that he has abandoned his post under a plea of having something important to communicate. When arrested, and ordered to write a defence and state his secret, it turns out to be merely a piece of advice to resort to a policy which, after trial, hail been decided against, þÿ probably | the rousing of the population against us. For all this, and much more which is minutely detailed, the Emperor agrees to the sentence of death passed upon Keying; but, inasmuch as it would give pain to him to see one who had once belli such an honourable position left in the market-place a headless corpse, Hienfung, in his boundless mercy, þÿ anxious to reconcile þÿ justice and þÿclemency, desires two high officers to visit Keying and request him to put himself to death. This strange mercy ran its course. Keying is dead. He was subtle, crafty, and false, and there is no great reason whv we should pity him ; but the Treaty of Nankin, which was so impoitant to us, was ruin to him, and his name must always be connected with t lie rise of British commerce m the extreme East.

In the fate of Keying we can read that the Tieaty of .Nankin was a more hitter medicine to Chinese pride than that which has just been concluded within hail of the capital. Not only was it the first step, but it had substantial points of difference from that of It Tien-sin surrendered Chinese territory. left Hong- It kong, Koulaugsoo, and Chusan in the hands of the barbarians; and, although the Court of Pekin does not often make a few millions of dollars a turning point in a negotiation, the sacrifice of 21 millions must have left some scar in the memory of a Chinaman. The Treaty of lit'ii sin, while it gives us all we want, does not cut very deep into the sensitive vanity of the race. The free transit was rather to be feared as a source of future danger than to be resented as the intrusion of a conqueror. Thu þÿ lanquci, or þÿ flitting þÿdevils, were always unquiet creatures ; they were always found scattered over the empire under some disguise. It is scarcely a uovclty to tolerate by treaty what lias in so many instances been tolerated by custom. Moreover, trading barbarians always bring a profit, and where profit is, there Imperial dignity will risk no collision with popular indignation. bis A Mussulman Proper would sell þÿProphet coffin, s of China if bo could get at it, for its weight in sycce. So, aaiti, the increase in the number of ports involves no sacrifice of the national pride. On the contrary, we have found at Swatow and elsewhere that Commerce can always recom-

mend herself to the good graces of the inhabitants of the city she is pleased to favour. Of the new ports upon the coast, the only one ol any novelty is that ofNcuchong, which has excited and baffled tile curiosity of sonic of our commercial readers. Some maps do not show it. It lies at the head of the Gulf of Liautung, and is the seaport of Moukdcn, and the natural entrepot of all Manchouria We arc told by those who have seen the place that the. trade to it, in Chinese vessels, is enormous, and we j know, from the nature of its exports, that the country abounds in pulse, beans, millet, barley, j of the and also timber and coal, all in of which are in full demand in the provinces of Shantung and Chili. From Neucliong and from Tongehou we shall be able effectually to work the trade of the Corea, where millions of men arc jammed together far closer than in China Proper ; and is it is important to observe that the climate one which requires thick clothing and does not produce cotton. January and February bring to the Corea a winter as severe as that of Canada ; and in the summer, while the denizens of Shanghai are almost in too great a state of lassitude to concoct a price-current, Neuehong, at the distance of three þÿdays steam, rejoices in her envirous of mountain scenery, wooded valleys, and a coast covered with a fine green turf. Throughout this negotiation the pervading spirit oil the part of the English and French has been one of generous forbearance. It must have been a great exercise of self-denial in Lord Elgin to turn back after exercising himself so often on the broad road which leads by an easy journey to Pekin. He might easily have forced his way there; and we presume lie has seen quite enough by this time to enable him utterly to despise the Sinologue vaticinations about the flight of the Emperor from Pekin, and the chaos that would follow upon the suicide of Hien-fung or a change of his dynasty. These prophecies have been repeated until their constant failures have rendered them at last ridiculous. Lord Elgin could doubtless have forced his way to Pekin had lie chosen. It was great moderation and great forbearance that lie did not do so, hut it was a sound judgment. As it stands, there is nothing in this Treaty of Tien-sin which carries a deep wound with it. The Earthquake is Mexico. þÿ The earthquake that took place in Mexico on the l'Jth of June last was one of the most severe that has been known since the Spanish invasion. At 9 þÿo clock in the morning shock came from the south. a This was followed by three more violent shocks from the same direction. Then four more shocks equally severe from the east, and after then a few tremblings. In the city of Mexico the strongest structures reeled to their foundations, the water spouted in jets from the sewers ; the street quarter of a minute. lamps vibrated from east to west for in a The earth opened the streets ; trees writhed and swayed for many minutes, and some were thrown out

ofthe earth. Houses, aqueducts, and railroads were seriously injured. About 24 towns and cities in Mexico sustained damage from the earthquake, and a great number of lives were lost. Damage to the value of more than a million sterling lias been done to the city of Mexico. All the violent shocks took place in the space of about one minute and a half. The shocks and tremblings lasted about three minutes.

THE TSETSE. A few remarks on the Tsetse, or Glossina morsitans, may here be appropriate. It is not much larger than the common housefly, and is nearly of the same brown color as the common honey-bee ; the after part of the body has three or four yellow bars across it; the wings project beyond this part considerably, and it is remarkably alert, avoiding most dexterously all attempts to capture it with the hand at common temperatures ; in the cool of the mornings and evenings it is less agile. Its peculiar buzz when once heard can never be forgotten by the traveller whose means of locomotion are domestic animals ; tor it is well known that the bite of this poisonous insect is certain death to the ox, horse, and dog. In this journey, though we were not aware of any great number having at any time lighted on our cattle, we lost forty-three fine oxen by its bite. We watched the animals carefully, and believe that not a score of flies were ever upon them. A most remarkable feature in the bite of the tsetse is its perfect harmlessness in man and wild animals, and even calves, so long as they continue to suck the cows. We never experienced the slightest injury from them ourselves, personally, although we lived two months in their habitat, which was in this case as sharply defined as in many others, for the south bank of the Chobe was infested by them, and the northern bank, where our cattle were placed, only fifty yards distant, contained not a single specimen. This was the more re-

markable, as we often saw natives carrying over raw meat to the opposite bank with many tsetse settled upon it. The does not seem to be injected by sting, or a by ova placed beneath the skin ; for, when one is allowed to feed freely on the hand, it is seen to insert the middle prong of three portions, into which the proboscis divides, somewhat deeply into the true skin ; it then draws it out a little way, and it assumes a crimson color as the mandibles come into brisk operation. The previously shrunken belly swells out, and, ii left undisturbed, the fly quietly departs when it is full. A slight itching irritation follows,

quito. In the ox this same bite produces no more immediate effects than in man. It does not startle him as the gad-fly does ; but a few days afterward the following symptoms supervene : the eye and nose begin to run, the coat stares as if the animal were cold, a swelling appears under the jaw, and sometimes at the navel ; and, though the animal continues to graze, emaciation commences, accompanied with a

afterward, purging comes on, and the animal no longer able to graze, perishes in a state of extreme exhaustion. Those which are in good condition often perish soon after the bite is inflicted with staggering and blindness, as if the brain were affected

- 0 P I A Vy Ij s . the progress of the complaint ; but, in general, the emaciation goes on uninterrupt- j edly for months, and, do what we will, the poor animals perish miserably. When opened, the cellular tissue on the surface of the body beneath the skin is seen to be injected with air, as if a quantity of soap-bubbles were scattered over it, or a dishonest, awkward butcher had been trying to make it look fat. The fat is of a greenish-yellow color and of an oily,, consistence. All the muscles are flabby, and the heart often so soft that the fingers may be made to meet through it. The lungs and liver partake of the disease. The stomach and bowels are pale and empty, and the gall-bladder is distended with bile. These symptoms seem to indicate what is probably the case, a poison in the blood, the germ of which enters when the proboscis is inserted to draw blood. The poisongerm, contained in a bulb at the root of the proboscis, seems capable, although very minute in quantity, of reproducing itself, for the blood after death by tsetse is very small in quantity, and scarcely stains the hands in dissection. I shall have byand-by to mention another insect, which by the same operation produces in the human subject both vomiting and purging. The mule, ass, and goat enjoy the same immunity from the tsetse as man and the game. Many large tribes on the Zambesi can keep no domestic animals except the goat, in consequence of the scourge existing in their country. Our children were

frequently bitten, yet suffered no harm ; and we saw around us numbers of zebras, buffaloes, pigs, pallahs and other antelopes, feeding quietly in the very habitat of the tsetse, yet as undisturbed by its bite as oxen are when they first receive the fatal poison poison. There is not so much difference in the natures of the horse and zebra, the buffalo and ox, the sheep and antelope, as to afford any satisfactory explanation of the phenomenon. Is a man not as much a domestic animal as a dog ? The curious feature in the case, that dogs perish though fed on milk, whereas the calves escape so long as they continue sucking, made us imagine that the mischief might be produced by some plant in the locality, and not by tsetse; but Major Vardon, of the Madras Army, settled that point by riding a horse up to a small hill infested but not more than in the bite of a mus- ! by the insect without allowing him time to graze, and, though he only remained long enough to take a view of the country and catch some specimens of tsetse on the animal, in ten days afterward the horse was dead. The well-known disgust which the tsetse shows to animal excreta, as exhibited when a village is placed in its habitat, has been observed and turned to account by some of the doctors. They mix droppings of animals, human milk, and some medicines to peculiar flaccidity of the muscles, and this I gether, and smear the animals that are proceeds unchecked until perhaps months about to pass through a tsetse district ; but

this, though it proves a preventive at the time, is not permanent. There is no cure yet known for the disease. A careless herdsman allowing a large number of cattle to wander into a tsetse district loses all except the calves ; and Sebituane once lost by it. Sudden changes of temperature nearly the entire cattle of his tribe, very produced by falls of rain seem to hasten many thousands, by unwittingly coming

under its influence. Inoculation does not insure immunity, as animals which have been slightly bitten in one year may perish by a greater number of bites in the next ; but it is probable that with the increase of guns the game will perish, as has happened in the south, and the tsetse, deprived of food, may become extinct simultaneously with the larger animals. þÿ Livingstone's travels in Africa.

TURKEY.

Athens, Sept. 7. On the night of the 4th inst., the Turks in Candia again made a display, and in such a manner as led the Governor to believe that the massa o of the Christians was intended. Great excitement prevailed. A letter dated Berat, a town in Albania, the 9th of September, informs us that the Governor of Monastir had just discovered a conspiracy among the Turks in that town to massacre all the Christians. The following are the details of the conspiracy. Three Sheiks bad for some

time been travelling through Albania and Epirus endeavouring to excite the population. They were well received at Aolone by the Mudir Salim Bey. These three fanatics succeeded in forming at Monastir a conspiracy which embraced 5,000 Turks, whoso plan was to fall suddenly ou the Christians on the 27th of August, when they should be assembled in their churches. All was ready, arms and ammunition, and it only remained to gain over a Bey who exercises great influence in that country. One of the Sheiks called on the Bey and told him that he was the bearer of an order from the Sheik Oul Silan, commanding all the faithful to contribute to the destruction of the infidels, and that 500 redifs were among the conspirators. The Bey pretended to assent to the proposition, but when the Sheik left him lie hastened to denounce the conspiracy to the Governor. The latter commanded that the chiefs of the conspiracy should be arrested, but one of the Sheiks contrived to escape. The redifs have been sent from Monastir, and have been replaced by regular troops.

In the last Anti-Slavery Reporter, is a Lotter liuited States Marshal and Mr. Rainey in getting j addressed by our Governor, Mr. llincks, to C. the negroes on board the frigate, which lay 18 | Tappan, Esqr., a gentleman from Boston, who visited Barbados some months ago, with a view to enquire into the results of Emancipation. The Letter is too long for insertion to-day ; we content ourselves with making some extracts, in which Mr. Hincks' opinions are given on subjects connected with the labouring classes, to which the attention of tho public lias recently been drawn. As to tho of charge usually brought against our labourers indolence, be does not agree in the fairness of it. lie says (rather awkwardly) þÿ "There is no doubt that the condition of the labouring classes ought to bo worse in Barbados than in any of the other Colonies," and yet the number of small pro-

prietors, holding less than five acres of laud, increased in sixteen years from 1,100 to 3,537 þÿ: " I shall now proceed to tho consideration of the complaint against the Creoles of African descent, that they are indolent, and that they

is a subject involved in much greater difficulty than the one on which I have already treated. 1 admit that the planters generally in several of the British colonies would vehemently maintain the correctness of this charge. I am, however, bound to affirm that, after a most patient investigation, 1 have been unable to arrive at such a conclusion. There is no doubt that the condition of the labouring classes ought to be worse in Barbados tliau in any of he other colonies. In Barbados, land is ex- .tantly dear, being worth, in small qualities, from 400 to COO dollars per acre. Wages are from lOd to Is per day as I have already stated. There are only five working days in the week, except during crop time. With all these disadvantages, the small proprietors in this Island, holding less than five acres of laud, increased in sixteen years from about 1,100 to 3,537. I doubt much whether such a proof of industrious habits could be furnished with regard to a similar class of labouiers in any had, it appears, taken the supreme power other country in the world. I think that in those colonies in which the sugar estates have been partially abandoned, wo must look to other causes than the indolence of the labourers. In all those colonics land is abundant, and comparatively cheap, and I need not remind any ono acquainted with the settlement of land in America, whether in the United States or the British Provinces, that where land is cheap and abundant labour will be dear aud scarce. The poor Irish immigrant pursues ex-

actly the same cour.-e in Canada which the Creole of African descent does in Guiana or Trinidad. He endeavours to get land of his own, and to become a proprietor instead of a labourer." With regard to religion and education, ho thinks that tho progress made since emancipation " quite equal to what could reasonably be expected.'" Au opinion to which all reflecting persons will subscribe, altho' at variance with the Letters of Meliora : þÿ " With regard to the condition of the African race, 1 can answer your queries with unmixed satisfaction, and with the conviction that there will he little if any difference of opinion among well-informed persons on that subject. The improvement which has taken place in the religious condition of the people of all classes, aud the progress of education, are quite equal to what could reasonably have been expected. The Creoles are advancing papidly in civilization. Yon have yourself made the acquaintance of who were formerly slaves, and now in independent circumstances, and enjoying large share of public respect. a But the very causes which have led to the pipes extend all over the ship, of so that on it great prosperity of the planters of Barbados have been to a considerable extent unfavourable to the labouring classes. If any of that class in the British West Indies had cause to complain, it would be in this Island; and it may be observed, that they can emigrate in a very few hours, and at very little expense, to colonies where land is both abundant and cheap, and

where higher wages prevail." Again, with regard to the social and political condition of the labouring classes, lie says þÿ: " There are no taxes peculiarly affecting the labourers. The elective franchise is generally high, but there are no class distinctions. Tho prejudices about colour arc, I think, fast dying away. Strangers are apt to exaggerate tho social distinctions, and to attributo the prejudices regarding race, or colour, to what proceeds from entirely different causes. Tho classes of society are more marked in the West Indies than they arc iu America."

Whatever be the result of the difference which has arisen between France and Portugal there are in it many things on which the mind of a well-wisher to the general peace of Europe, and to the great interests of humanity at large, must rest with little satisfaction. The circumstances appear very simple, and, indeed, on the facts there is very little dispute. A French vessel, the Charles et Georges, is found by the Portuguese authorities of Mozambique on a part of the coast interdicted to the approach of foreigners, because an approach to it in that particular point is regarded by the Portuguese Government as almost conclusive evidence of an attempt to carry on the Slave Trade. On board the ship were one hundred and ten negroes and a delegate of the French Government. The delegate and captain stated to the Portuguese authorities, that the men were there by their own free consent, having engaged themselves to go as labourers to the island of Reunion, that the negroes had regular passports from the authorities at Mozambique, and that the vessel was lying off the interdicted portion of the coast tor the purpose of obtaining a surgeon. To this it was answered by the Portuguese, that a surgeon was to be found at Mozambique, and was not to be found on that part of the coast. The negroes were examined, and declared one and all that they were carried off against their will and not in virtue of any agreement, and the passports spoken of turned out to be documents furnished

by a native chief, who probably was the person from whom the negroes were obtained. Under tbese circumstances the vessel was seized as a slaver and sent to Lisbon for adjudication. On hearing of this the French Government have sent two men-of-war to the Tagus to wake with the thunder of their guns the echoes of the Rock of Lisbon, have peremptorily demanded the surrender of the Charles et Georges within forty-eight hours, have given orders to the fleet at Toulon to hold itself in readiness to sail, and twice verbally refused the offer of the Portuguese Government to submit the matter to the arbitration of a third Power. The latest accounts hold out a hope, indeed, that a friendly arrangement may be expected, but matters are stiil in an uncertain state. The ground on which the French Government is understood to reply is that the presence of a French delegate on board the ship necessarily implied such absolute innocence of any design of Slave-trading that the Portuguese Government was bound to be satisfied with it at once, and to inquire no further, and that compared with this conclusive proof all matters of suspicion or irregularity become absolutely insignificant, and ought to be thrown aside as of no account whatever. To us the mere merits of this controversy, assuming the facts to bo correctly stated above, appear to present no difficulty whatever. We know not what proof can be required of an offence of this kind if the facts which wc have just alleged are not to be held sufficient. The

vessel was found in flagrant delict, with the negroes actually on board her, and they stated, when examined, that they were there, not by their own free will, but under the compulsion of superior force. If it be said that the captain and delegate were deceived in the matter and believed these people to have gone on board voluntarily in pursuance of an agreement to labour in the colony of Reunion which they fully understood, we may ask why the ship was taken to an unusual and interdicted station, why an utterly absurd reason was given for her going there, and why false statements were made with regard to passports from the Portuguese authorities at Mozambique ? These things showed not only that the French captain and delegate were doing wrong, but that they knew it, and, coupled with the fact that they had a hundred and ten negroes on board, male out as complete a case as the nature of the transaction could possibly admit. To all this the French had nothing to oppose except a conclusive presumption invented by themselves, that it is absolutely impossible for a delegate of the French Government to lend himself to a slave-trading transaction ; and that, therefore, such a transaction must be assumed to be impossible whatever evidence there be to the contrary. We are not aware that the law of nations recognizes as one of its principles the absolute impeccability and incorruptibility of the

agent of a foreign Government, or considers that Government to be entitled, by placing a delegate on board a ship bearing i "< ag, to give that ship a licence to violate with impunity the obligations of treaties and the police regulations of a friendly State. We, therefore, feel no difficulty in concluding that on the merits of the question the great Power is entirely in the wrong, and the little one is entirely in the right. This, however, is but a very small part of the matter. Let us assume France to have been as clearly right as she was manifestly wrong. Surely, in order to enforce that right, she should have uttered no menaces and employed no measures which she would not have used to Russia, to England, or to the United States of America. If France believed herself to bo in the right, in what respect could her dignity suffer if, instead of the intolerable pretension to be judge in her own cause, she had shown herself ready to abide by the impartial decision of a neutral Power ? If she knew she was wrong, no doubt the course adopted is explicable enough, but it is not the less an invasion of that equality which the public law of modern Europe attributes to all sovereign States, and an infraction of the Paris Congress which binds the great Powers to have recourse to the intervention of an impartial arbitrator before appealing to arms. No doubt it is exceedingly convenient for nations as well as individuals to decide their own causes in their own favour, but the time will

often come when the inexpediency of this onesided method of adjudication is made manifest even to those who are most inclined to have recourse to it. The doctrine that justice is only for equals, but that between superior and inferior relations are to be regulated by their relative powers alone, finds no acceptance in the code of modern Europe, and any Power that succeeds in introducing it will have shaken to their foundations those doctrines upon which alone a general peace can be permanently maintained. We cannot but regard it as unfortunate that infractions, real or supposed, of the international law of Europe with regard to the Slave Trade should so frequently form the occasion of differences to which France is a party. We might have hoped that a nation which claims, not unreasonably, a foremost place in directing the march of civilization. would, even if she bad been subjected to a slight amount of unmerited annoyance and vexation by the honest efforts of other countries to put a complete end to the Slave Trade, have considered the excellent end in view as a complete excuse for any irregularity in the means taken to attain it, and would have always been satisfied with proof that the dispute arose front endeavours made iu good faith to put down this abominable traffic. Unhappily the exact contrary seems to be the case, and nothing excites the indignation of the department over which Count Walewski presides so much as an honest and unselfish attempt to avert the most hideous
cruelty that even the thirst of gain itself ever prompted or defeuded.

The Indian telegrams give us only the recurring details of a known general truth. You cannot throw down a glass vase, or put your elbow through a window pane, without incurring some cuts and scratches from the fragments before they are all picked up and carried away. We have broken, dispersed, and utterly disorganized a force which was sufficient in its integrity to hold 150,000,000 of people in subjection, and to defend their country against any outward enemy. We could not kill them all. With vivid recollection of their treachery and their atrocities wc still say, Heaven forbid that such a tremendous immolation should stain our history ! Wc must kill a great many þÿ wc have killed a great many ; but we may hope to drive a very large portion back to the occupation of tilling the earth. This, however, will only be gradually done. The first process is to break up the organized armies, the next is to hunt the guerrilla parties ; these will naturally subdivide into gangs of robbers, and with constant pursuit these again will gradually melt away; þÿ the members of these gangs will tiud robbery a dangerous and unprofitable business, and tbe land will then assume its former aspect of peace and security This, however, is a process. The end is only to be gained by a succession of labours, and we cannot expect to see it attained at a single coup. The news just receivod is precisely what might have been expectod under the circumstances, and we may bo

thankful that we have not to set against our many small successes one single reverse. It is remarkable, as illustrative of the ignorance and credulity of the enemy with whom we have to deal, that even at this twelfth hour, when the mutineers have no stronghold in their possession, when there is no rebel army in the Held, no standard to which the disaffected can turu their steps, little mutinies are still happening. Anybody would have supposed that who two regiuieuts of Bengal Native Infantry the paraded without their arms at Mooltan were well informed of the utterly desperate condition of the cause of the insurgents, and that, instead of wishing to cast in their lot with the armed rebels, they would rather have from themselves that they were safe congratulated any share of their terrible chastisement. They must have been told that the rebel cause was prospering, and they must have believed it. Some holy Pundits and fanatical Dervishes must have got among them, and persuaded them that the stories of English victories were all fables, and that their brethren with a victorious army were marching down to their assistance. These were certainly the convictions at Barrackpore and Dumdum until a very recent date. The disarmed Sepoys would not credit the testimony of their own senses against the wild exhortations of their holy men. They had been told, and they believed, that the English troops who marched thr mgli those station, or who were carried by the railway on the opposite side of the Ganges

and in sight of their cantonments, were only a small body of men, who were marched and countermarched, and who were carried to and fro, up and down the railway, to give an appearance of a force which did not exist. They believed in the approach of Nana Sahib with a powerful army as firmly as the Jews believe iu th.e coining of their Messiah. We must not wonder, therefore, that small bodies still hold out obstinately, or that we have still to keep armed watch over the disarmed regiments. The audacity of impenetrable ignorance is always formidable, and there is a desperate credulity which coun.s no odds and seems to thrive best upon impossibilities. In no other way can we account for the mutiny of these Mooltan troops. Toe gross improbability of such a rising might not unnaturally have caused a slackening of precautions and it is a very important circumstance that the outbreak was so promptly and severely repressed. The soundness of the Bombay Army i- also still shown to be proof against treacherous solicitations. It does seem absurd that after recent events at Gwalior even the Nana should | be so simply sanguine as to despatch emissaries to the very troops who had seen this stronghold taken, and to attempt to induce them to join a cause which they had themselves found to be so desperate of chances. Doubtless, ho knows his countrymen best, and where ho sees hope we must not relax precaution. The Gwalior fugitives, who could not hold their own behind the walls of the strongest fortress in India, were nut

likely to be formidable in flight. They arc, however, the debris of the toughest native force we have met with during all this servile war. The troops of the native Rajahs do not care to oppose them ; they easily gather the native levies to their standards; they occupy the cities that lie upon their line of flight, and only succumb to European forces Defeated by General Roberts tlicy fled southwards, captured the treasure, the guns, and the city of the Rajah of Jhalra Patun; and then, mowing towards Bhopal, were met and defeated by General Michel, who retook nearly all the guns, and again dispersed the fugitive army. There is a mountainous district south of the scone of this battle in which these mutineers will perhaps find refuge, and where they might probably be blocked up. Even in its flight and its dispersion this body of mutineers has exhibited a fertility of resources and a choice of leaders which make it very desirable that they should be entirely broken up. It is satisfactory to know that forces are being directed from several quarters upon the district they now occupy. The decisive scouring of all the infested parts of Ilindostan will, however, soon come. Lord Clyde must quickly he upon the field of action, perhaps he is already there, with 25,000 British Infantry and 10,000 Cavalry, a good portion of which will also be British. There is no rebel force in India which can withstand those troops for one hour. We hope there is no body which can evade them. It is, however, evident that it
is not a pitched battle or a great victory which

$ f » pj 8; 0) (i ft ft (1 ft will put an end to these mutinies, or fix in the Indian mind the fact of the uselessness of future resistance. Up to this time the recollections of a mutinous Sepoy are of a checkered character. If he has upon his memory fields of frightful carnage and charges which none of his race could hope to resist, he has had some bright moments of revenge, and he has also obtained a very considerable quantity of plunder. This latter will eventually be his greatest danger, for when the dispersion has become a little more complete a Sepoy will be hunted by his own countrymen for the gold inohurs which he is now universally believed to Lave concealed about him, just as a civet cat is hunted for its civet. It is not, however, yet quite come to this, and the game has still some charms. We hope there may soon be safe opportunity of showing these insurgents that submission is not the same thing as death, and that their true interest is to lay down their arms and go back to their villages. It will probably then bo our true policy to be deaf to the officious spies who will be ready enough to point out the skulking inutiueer, and to pour a general amnesty over the land; but the war has not yet arrived at this crisis. While regiments are still rising in mutiny, and while native forces are deserting their own chiefs to join a mutineer invading torce, it is quite certain the necessary impression has not been made, or that it has not been spread so widely as the case requires. The rains are now over and the time for active

operations is commencing. Between this and next March there will be an interval fully sufficient for all that has to be done. It is a good symptom that the police force is already mentioned as doing execution upon these scattered bands, and we hope the time is not far distant when we shall bear of no further necessity for moving guns and regiments against this broken mob. When the public peace can be preserved by the civil force we may turn to other discussions beating upon this great country, and, having seen how b st it may be coerced, proceed to the solution of the more pleasant problem, how best it may be improved.

Mr Editor ! From the last published þÿ Extract of tho proceedings of the Burgher Council of St. Croix ' it is seen, that, among others, Mr. Bertram van Beverhoudt lias been granted a pension of $3 from the Ruin Fund. Mr v. Beverhoudt has þÿoil s Office for upwards of 30 Burgher served faithfully as clerk in the years. XVhen Conn the messenger in the þÿGovernment s-offiee, Mr Kemp, was compelled to resign from old age, about 10 years ago, he received a pension of $100 a year to comfort his remaining days The comparison does not speak much for the liberality of the Burgher Council And mark ! The pittance allowed Mr. v. Beverhoudt has not been granted from tho Landtreasury ; although the Landtreasury has a well stocked chest, although its revenues have of late come in so abundantly as to leave a sur- Council has not as much as a couple of Burgher plus of many Thousands, yet the dollars a month to spare to support the declining years of an old and faithful servant, when infirmity and reedy circumstances compel him to solicit its charity. No, the pension in question has been granted Mr. v. Beverhoudt from the Rum fund. From a Fund expressly set apart by Royal Ordinance for the support of widows or orphan children, the Burgher Council, under whose special care the Rum Fund has been placed, has not hesitated to remunerate one of their own ci-devant officers, au individual who, do doubt, will be willingly admitted by every member of tho community, to have a well founded claim on relief

from the Landtreasury ; but who certainly neither has nor can ever obtain any such claim on the Rum Fund. And this has been done by the Burgher Council under whose special care, as observed, the Rum Fund has been placed, and who consequently should bo foremost to see that the regulations of the fund be strictly attended to. In coutravention of these regulations the Burgher Council has not hesitated to withhold from widows and orphans what ought to have been Rhared to them, in order to screen the

Landtreasury from a comparatively trifling outlay, which, if just and right in itself, and duly approved of by the Council, evidently should be paid from the Landtreasury, and from no other source whatever. How can such a proceeding, such a deviation from the rules laid down for the application of the means of a public fund entrusted to the Burgher þÿCouncil scare, be defended ? It is hardly to be supposed that the Honorable Board could be ignorant of the dictates of a law, which by all means they should know. From whatsoever source the irregularity springs þÿ might it not be considered witbin the province of the Government to take the matter in hand and set it right 1 Remaining yours respectfully, A Friend of truth and justice,

CHRISTIANSTED, ST. CROIX. TUESDAY, 16th NOVEMBER, 1S5S. Our columns have lately contained communications of a nature which shows a strong and growing inclination to investigate and expose public abuses. This i-nclination, it must be borne in mind, is limited in its action through the trammels of a public censorship. Abuses can nevertheless increase to such an extent as to force expression from a public otherwise apathetic to a perilous degree. While the course which has been adopted, of writing newspaper articles, may, certainly, have its influence, by awakening interest in the matter ; yet we are not so sanguine as to suppose that any of the authorities will be led to frame new laws for the correction of t hose abuses merely from the perusal of these articles. There is a surer path open to the public to express their desire for reform. Let public meetings be held, and let petitions be framed and presented in such quarters where they will be heard. It is idle to wait until some independent, and so-called man of influence, steps forward to head the movement. Call the meeting yourselves þÿ and let it be pre-eminently a meeting poor men, who feel the effects of of heavy taxation and receive no compensating advantages. A new Burgher Council will soon have to be elected; and the Colonial Council, all powerful as it is for taxation, yet impotent for good, must, we suppose, soon be in session, if it be not defunct ; let therefore some timely measures be taken to exercise a legal, yet powerful, pressure on these bodies ; so that
the wishes of the community shall no longer be disregarded. From the St Thomas Times, 30th Nov. 1858

Up to a late hour on Saturday night the electrician had been unable to discover the precise locality where the interruption of the electric current takes place. In the letter written by Mr. Whitehouse, the late electrician of the company, that gentleman holds out the hope that the damage which has taken place would be found to be hut at a short distance from the shore, and could be easily repaired by the substitution of the larger cable intended for the shore end of the telegraph. This heavy portion of the cable, weighing about six tons to the mile, or rather more than six times the weight of the lino which has already been laid, is at present lying at Keyham. It was not taken on board' the Agamemnon, for so improbable seemed the chance of the successful submergence of the cable, that it was not deemed necessary to send the shore end to Valentia until the result of the second attempt was ascertained. As soon as the communication had been established, orders were sent for the shipment of the shore end, and the Bilboa steamer was sent to Keyham to take it round to Valentia. While engaged in putting the cable on hoard a message was unexpectedly received to discontinue the process, and leave it still at Keyham. This message was, we understand, forwarded from Valentia, as it was found by the electrical tests which were applied that the interruption of the communica ion was not within such a distance of the shore ns would admit of the fault being remedied by the substitution of the heavier cable. The

shore end of the telegraph is that which is most exposed to the action of the sea, and with respect to which the greatest fears were enter- I tained by the public ; but it turns out that this portion is perfect, and that the defective part is at a point much fnithcr distant from the land. To many persons it will appear impossible, by j any mechanical or other scientific arrangement, to ascertain tlio spot at which the continuity of an electric current may cease. It is difficult 1 enough to conceive the practicability of transmitting an electric spark along two or three thousand miles of wire, or even through a much shorter distance. But this is done every day, and we have less doubt that the subtle fluid which starts from London will reach Edinburgh, or the place to which it is directed, than that the railway train will reach its prescribed ter- 1 minus But to ascertain the spot at which the lightning leaves its track, and escip s into the depths of the Atlantic, is a task which would appear to he even more difficult than for the j manager at Euston station to learn, without the aid of telegraph or other communication, the place where the expre.-s train had left the line by sonic unhappy accident, after it had started on its journey to the north. Strange as it may seem, the electrician has the power of ascertaining, hy means of the electric fluid itself, the locality of the tiny outlet, by which it escapes into the sea. Some time since a most ingenious piece of mechanism was made, hy winch the

electricity could he weighed, the fluid being made to act upon a magnet ; and this, upon the, end of a nicely-poised steelyard, would tell with accuracy the weight of (he current transmitted from the other end of a wire at a long distance. Following out this experiment, we believe first shown by Professor Faraday, at the Royal Institution, other electricians have arranged a very sensitive piece of machinery, hy which the amount of resistance opposed to the passage of the electricity by the conducting wire may be correctly ascertained. The amount of resistance offered through the whole length of the Atlantic cable, or oven one half of it, is something very much larger than any which can he marked hy the delicate machinery hitherto employed upon shorter distances of wire. The consequence is that the electricians have not yet been able satisfactorily to ascertain the place where the cable is defective. Of one thing, however, they arc certain, that is, that the fault does not occur within twenty or thirty miles of the land, and we are

informed that within the first two or three hundred miles the continuity is still perfect and complete. Beyond this distance all is still doubt and uncertainty, and it is idle at present to speculate upon the subject. Should the defect he found to exist in the deep parts of the sea, the public must he content to hear that lor the present the Atlantic Telegraph is a failure. It will not be possible to raise the sunken portion of the wire, or repair it, when laid in great depths. Within a few miles of the shore the wire may be under-run ; hut when it has been sunk at the depth of two or three miles below the surface, the great length of cable which would be suspended, and the resistance which the water would give to its rising, would produce a strain upon the wire much greater than its strength would hear. A cable which would he strong enough to sustain its own weight while sinking, might not possess the requisite strength to admit of its being hauled up through the water. þÿ Observer. The Debats publishes the following letter addressed to it hy M. Babiuet, of the Institute of France: þÿ Your readers may have seen tha I was one of the first to prouounce the success of laying down the Transatlantic telegraph to he something miraculous. The event was the more meritorious that, in a recent conversation with one of the heads of the French telegraph lines, we agreed that it was uearly impossible to obtain a satisfactory working from a conductor of that kind. In fact, the electric cur-

rent hy running along a metallic wire, and particularly one enveloped in other metallic wires, produces a powerful electric charge which, in freeing itself, gives signals completely foreign to the despatch. The only remedy is to wait patiently until everything has become again calm, which requires a considerable time. It is nearly the same as what would occur in a room where there is a very Btrong echo, and where a person speaking would be obliged to stop at each word. This embarrassment had already occurred on a small scale in the line across the English Channel ; hut the weakness of the electric return currents allowed the inconvenience to he got over hy the use of a magnetic apparatus which was not too easily uffected. The telegraph to Algeria already suffers materially from this þÿcause. From the Fond on Star of September 14th. Tho Paris correspondent of the Times, writing on Monday evening, says : þÿ ,l The Ministerial papers speak of the indemnity, without arbitration, to bo paid by Portugal. The Moniteur says nothing of this. It is whispered that Portugal protests against the injustice which site is too weak to repel. J , A case has lately occurred in this place, under which a comparatively heavy fine was imposed on a lady arriving from New York for bringing a few letters for individuals residing here along with her in her trunk, in which she deposited them, as the American Post-Office, not being in communication with ours, or perhaps not having the remotest on ence, had placed no mail-bag idea of its exist- board in which the individual might have felt herself bound to deposit those letters. On her coming ashore and delivering her trunks to be searched the letters were taken out by a Custoin-House Officer and handed to the Postmaster, who, for some reason, refused to receive them. This manner of proceeding on the part of the lady, it must be remarked, being the only one left open to her, and bciug, we think, in perfect accordance with the 15 b of the" Postal Ordinance, has been observed on many other previous occasions without leading to such unpleasant results. The measure adopted by the authorities, by which the individual has been fined, appears to us to be harsh in the extreme ; especially as we are unable to see how that individual can be considered as having infringed the right of the Post-Office. At best, this right to claim foreign letters and of charging postage on them appears to us to be very doubtful; and, in its application to the present case, pretty unfounded; since all that could be expected of the individual was performed. The Postal Law we must acknowledge is a

very elaborate affair, as prolix as if meant for the British Empire. But it wants a very important necessary þÿ we mean, appliances to effect its ends. Where are the conventions with foreign Governments for the transmission of letters ? Where are the vessels, steam or sailing, to carry the Mail Bags ? Not a single cent is expended by our Government for the benefit of the Public iu this respect ; but, on the contrary, every advantage is taken of private enterprise to effect the ends of the law. This however is in such perfect keeping with the spirit pervading the whole law that wc cease to wonder at it. Wc may be allowed to express a doubt, whether, out of China, a law placnig such trammels

S T-. CROIX AVIS, on the free inter-change of thought, þÿ a law so downright opposed to the exigencies of the present age, þÿ a law so justly condemned by every liberal mind, þÿ could be conceived by any legislative body but the Colonial Council of St. Croix.

The cutter sailed from New York on the 19ili of August, and occupied forty-five days in the voyage. She is only 45 tons burden, 53 feet in length over all, 44 keel, 1 1> feet in width, and the mast is 50 feet 6 indies long. She has not raised bulwarks, the deck being merely protected by a stout rope sustained by iron stanchions, est draught of water is 6 feet. " A more frail- ller greatlooking bark in which to cross the stoiniy Atlantic (says a person who saw her at Southampton) it is scarcely possible to conceive; and, as she lies off the town quay, surrounded by the larger craft built for the purposes of our river and coast, few would imagine, or scarcely believo it when told them, that this miniature vessel could have travelled over such a wild waste of waters." The Christopher Columbus was built at Stain" ford, Connecticut, in seven mouths, every part of the work, except the stepping of the mast and the rigging, being executed by Webb himself, even to the cutting down and shaping of the timber with which she is constructed.
