He bears on his Lead au earthen vessel of palmoil, or carries two or three quills of golddust, the result of his own industry iu washing the saud after the rains Ilis sole article of clothing is a Manchester rcrnal, or length of checkered cotton, girded round his loins. But ho knows the value of his own merchandise, aud of that for which he iuteuds to exchange it. He is a bird by uo means to be caught with chaff, lie will not change his palmoil for a bunch of feathers, nor his gold for a string of beads ; neither does he affect any article of European clothing, nor hanker alter any produce of European civilization. 11c wants rum þÿ the strong, coarse American rum þÿ aud he knows to a teaspoon ful how much he ought to get of it. He wants from time to time a new remal, also a cloth or blanket to throw over his shoulders on State occasions, and a musket to make a row with and fire off when lie keeps custom. But he wants no food, because the maize springs up for liiui almost without cultivation, and bis women pound it between two stones, and add water to make a paste which be calls kankee, and on tliis lie gorges himself with great relish. Sometimes his soul lustcth for meat, and then the black snails of the forest, as

big as a fist, furnish him with a soup of which provident palm oil housewife is also an essential ingredient. The threads these snails on a bit of grass and dries tlieni in the sun, thus saving her lord and master from the toil of putting out his hand to take them. The long black-haired monkey also provides him with a bounteous repast. Pity the sorrows of a European tray lling through the bush and partaking of the hospitality lie will have to pay handsomely for it) of a native, when, as a delicacy reserved for him , there is fished up out of the big pot of soup a black head with the lips drawn back, and the white teeth grinning, and such a painful resemblance of the faces arouud him that for a moment he woudcrs which of the youDger members of the family has been sacrificed to the exigencies of the occasion. But he is reassured, and discovers that he is not eating man, but monkey. The native of the Gold Coast has no desire to buy a house, nor to build a house, nor to live in a house. Signorina Lavinia Bandini, aided by her father and several gentlemen Amateurs, with Mr. Moeser presiding at the Piano, made her first appearance on Saturday evening last, and was received by the audience with constant applause and frequent encores. There is no doubt that Miss Bandini is a Violinist of very rare excellence, which is the more appreciated for her youth, ease and grace with which she manages the instrument. Doubtless the instrument equally well executed, (which however, might be doubted), put in the hands of a cross looking old spinster, would fail to produce anything like the same effect. M iss Bandini, we are informed, has been induced to give another Concert, previous to her leaving the Island, and of which due notice will be given. The public on that occasion, we are disposed to believe, will not refuse to afford her that patronage which her skill so fully entitles her to receive. þÿ St. Thomas Times.

s T c R o ij x A y u s From the London Times, November 1(1. About four weeks since we may presume that there began in India one of the most important campaigns in the history of this country. Certain it is that the operations which were to be undertaken at the setting in of the cold weather arc of a kind almost without precedent, and will form hereafter a fit subject of study for the military student. The object of the campaign is not to defeat the enemy and break his power, for that is done ; nor is it merely to disperse the beaten bauds, for it is of little use to disperse them if they can come together again a few miles off. It is to surround, to entrap, and to destroy as a military force a great number of little detached armies, each of which is powerless by itself against the smallest of our columns, but which in the aggregate compose a vast array of rebels, and, though they no longer threaten our power, may keep the country through which they range in disorder for months or years. It is a hopeless task to attempt an explanation of what Lord Clyde and his Generals purpose. The usual notion of a campaign is that one army occupies a lino of positions, and that the other advances against it with a view of driving it out by the capture of one or more strong places or the gaining of one or more victories. But a short examination of the state of things in Oude and the adjacent district disabuses the mind of any such notions. A plan of the country with the rebel positions shows at a glance the kind of warfare which we have to expect. Every

few mii there is a rebel camp, with a force varying, p< ps, from a thousand men to more than ten times that number. A short summary of the principal bands Lord Clyde and his lieutenants will have to destroy is sufficient for the general reader. At Churda, near the foot of the Himalayas, are N ina Sahib and Balarow, his brother, with 13,000 men of all arms and 20 guns. This is probably the largest force arrayed against us, unless, indeed, it be equalled by the often vanquished, but still surviving, army of Central India. About 15 miles East of Shahjehnnpore is Khan Bahadoor Khan, Nawab of Bareilly, with a considerable force, though, probably, far inferior to that of the Nana. At Khyrabad are 2,200 infantry, 300 cavalry, and 7 guns. Along the banks of the Ganges, from Furruckabad to near Cawnporo, are the little armies of eudul chiefs ; at a place called Sandec, for iusuuee, there are 600 infantry, 300 cavalry, uns ; at Thoolepore, 2,000 men, 4 guns ; Igraon, 2,500 men, 2 guns; at Birwa, 3,0-. men, 12 guns; at one place we have 3,000 moil " of all sorts," while at another there are 250 Sepoys and one gun as representatives of the rebellion. Some of the largest bodies arc more to the East, on the banks of the Gorga At Bonndee is the Begum with 6,500 men of all sorts and five guns ; at Futtehpore and Bitlilac arc 11,000 men and ten guns ; and a few miles from them 3,000 more. Further East we have, opposite Fyzabad, on the other side of the rivor, 6,000 Zemindaree men, while our ally, as we must now call him,

Maun Singh, supports our garrison with his following. At l'arsidepore are 3,000 iufaatry of all sorts, 1,200 cavalry, and 10 guns; at Amcalce is Rajah Lall Madho Singh with 1,900 infantry, 22 guns, and 3 mortars. We might continue this Homeric catalogue, hut the foregoing is enough to give a notion of what the enemy is like. It is evident that the force opposed to us is very considerable in the aggregate ; but it is equally plain that there is no master mind or even a common spirit to unite these scattered and independent levies ; that they consist chiefly of the ill-armed retainers of the Oude aristocracy, and that they will await each in its separate district the attack of the British columns. The number of guns still in the possession of the rebels is large, but it has been proved in action after action that they are unable to use them with effect, and that their artillery is really almost an assistance to us, as hampering their movements. The rebellion, then, may be considered as having entered into a defensive phase. The armed bands of the enemy may indeed plunder the country, each in its locality ; but as a whole they do not contemplate any attack on the British, but content themselves with holding the villages aud small towns, and there awaiting our operations. The task of Lord Clyde, of course, is to sweep them out of the country, so as to give tho landowners and people, now

coerced into complicity, an opportunity of returning to their allegiance. The plan of operations is fairly indicated in the official memorandum, which we publish in another place. From the West a column will advance from Bareilly and Shahjehanpore, clear Nowrungabad and the country now infested by Kalin Bahadoor Khan, and will proceed to establish itself at Seetapore. In the East a brigade is to keep the country open between Sultanporc and Fyzabad. West of Luoknow a brigade will move from Sundeela on Sandee, through one ol' the most thickly infested districts ; its duty, according to the memorandum, will be to clear the country to the Westward. All these various columns in the East, West, and North were, if the intentions of tlie Commander-in-Chief were carried out, to commence operations about the 15th of October. At Lucknow, Fyzabad, aud other places troops would be kept moveable to support the columns actively engaged. The completeness of the preparations made for the destruction of the enemy will be evident from the sketch we have made. Oude is a small country, and the little armies which bold the villages are often only a few miles apart. A British force well supplied and led by an active commander could in a few days drive out of their positions half a dozen of these petty bands. It is not as if long marches of weeks were necessary to come up with the rebels, and as if our most powerful enemies were weariness, hunger, and thirst. The field of' war is limited ; it is known to our Generals, the re-

sources of a great empire are at the disposal ol our Commissariat, and almost every mile of the distance has been traversed by European soldiers in the course of the present war. Lord Clyde has bad a year to meditate on the plan of campaign, and he has had tho assistance ot experienced Generals and of an army which is now pretty well inured to war. What doubt can there be, then, that this series of movements, begun on nearly the same day, carried out against a beaten and discouraged enemy, and according to a plan which will prevent the rebels from forming junctions of their forces at any point, will be speedily successful I From tho principal points which our troops hold, from Lucknow, Shahjehanpore, Fyzabad, Sultanpore, and other places, tile columns will simultaneously cut through the disaffected districts, so that each rebel army, or conglomeration of armies, will find itself driven from the defensive position which it lias taken up. The delive ranee of the villages and driving the enemy into the jungle will be the signal, we hope, for a general submission. It would be wrong, however, to persuade the public that the task of the British Army is complete, or even approaching completion. There the rebels are, and there thoy will remain for many a month longer Granted that the greater number of the men now in arms return to their families and occupations ; yet there will be thousands who will prolong their hostility to the British Government to the last moment of their lives. Such

men as thj Nana Sahib have put a gulf between themselves and English mercy ; and wo may expect that the leaders of the rebellion generally will fancy themselves without the pale of forgiveness, and persuade their followers that there is no hope for high or low. One of our greatest difficulties may, indeed, arise from the terrors of the enemy, who perhaps will never be convinced that when the English promise to pardon him they intend to keep their word. The unhappy kingdom of Oude is probably destined to bo the prey of desperate bands ol robbers long after the great Indian Mutiny has become matter of history. But, as the close of 1857 saw our Indian Empire saved by the capture of Luckuow and tho defeat of the two chief rebel armies, so the present year will, no doubt, witness the destruction of everything which can be justly called a hostile army, and tho complete restoration of civil government throughout India.

þÿ þÿ In the course of her history England has made many cessions of territory ; hut in later ages at least, these have been, saving the recognition of American independence, all voluntary. To vanquished enemies and unfortunate allies we have restored colonies and factories, the most thriving settlements and the most commanding harbours No,w we are called upon to n fre a

dependency to itself, or rather to abandon it, that it may amalgamate with another State with which its inhabitants feel more sympathy than with our own. Sir John Young, the Lord High Commissioner of the Ionian Islands, has addressed a despatch to the Home Government, advising in the plainest terms that the protectorate over five of the islands þÿ Ceplialonia, Zante, Ttlncn, Santa Maura, and Cciigo- -shall be given up, and the islands declared part of the neighbouring kingdom of Greece. In return for this concession to the desires of the people he thinks that we might convert Corfu and Paxo into Crown colonies, with such forms of administration as might seem best fitted to places retained only for military purposes. These propositions will, no doubt, at first startle the British public. It seems certaiuly a strange proceeding to yield to disaffection and sedition that which we declare is not demanded by justice. The Ionian Islands after having been occupied by Russia and by France, came legitimately under the government of Great Britain, and we can with a good conscience assert that wo have endeavoured to govern them faithfully and well. They have had institutions which carried freedom to its furthest possible limit ; their religion and usages have received every mark of respect from the governing State, and the Ionians themselves have had the protection of the British flag in ever- part of the Levant where they might wander. And yet because, without any tangible grievance, they have made year after year noisy

demonstrations of illwill, they are to obtain a release from their allegiance to England, which must be held to have received the Seven Islands in IS 15 as a compensation for vast efforts, and not a few territorial cessions. To such arguments there is indeed little to aaswer; and this country might with perfect equity retain its dominion over the islands while giving them a Government fitted to advance their prosperity and remedy any real grievance. We are not bound to satisfy fanciful wishes or to redress sentimental wrongs. But, as the Government of the Cape gave up the Orange lliver Settlement because its Dutch inhabitants persisted in showing antipathy to British rule, so it may be urged that wo should do a sensible thing in getting rid of the Ionians. 'I hey have no claim to an abandonment of the Protectorate ; they have been well treated, and their call for an union with Greece is not one to which the Protectorate is bound to listen. But, as they wish to go, and wc have no interest in keeping them, the abandonment, it is said, may as well be made. This, of course, is a question for the serious consideration of the Crown and Parliament of Great Britain. Any decided opinion at present would be premature, inasmuch as Mr. Gladstone is deputed to inquire, and only on his report can any resolution be taken. But the despatch of Sir J. Young deserves the attention of the public. The Lord High Commissiener congratulates the Government that the forbearing policy of many years has at last begun

to have its effect, and that the open violence of the Assembly has passed into a more sedate tone of remonstrance. The conclusion which lie draws from this improved state of things is, that England should take tho opportunity of withdrawing from tho greater part of the islands, and bringing Corfu, where our dominion has never been so hateful, under the immediate Government of tho Crown. It remains to be seen how far the alleged loyalty of Corfu and Paxo will consider itself recompensed by a measure which cuts them alone off from an union with Greece, which separates them from the other five islauds, and changes them front members of a protested

Cj i OH A\ V/ I) % republic into Crown possession of Great Britain, like Malta and Gibraltar. We cannot but think that if the absence of seditious speeches and articles is known to be accepted as a sign of attachment to England tho Ionians will take care that Corfu shall make her voice heard as loudly and violently as Zantc or Cephalonia. What will be the effect on the Greek, and indeed on all the Christian provinces of Turkey, wc do not presume to anticipate. When five dependencies of the British Crown have extorted their sur" render to another Power merely by long-continued importuuity and chronic disaffection the example is not likely to be lost on the Rayah subjects of the Empire to which we have guaranteed integrity of territory. Nor can wo think that Eugland will continue to hold Corfu on any high moral grounds after parting with the sister islands, if it be fitting that Greeks in Cephalouia should be united to tho Hellenic s.tock, it is equally fitting that Greeks in Corfu should not be kept out of the brotherhood. At prcseut we have a firm standing ; we say the islands are under our protection by the public law of Europe, and that tho identity of race gives them 110 more claim to political unity with King Otho's dominions than it gives to Macedonia or Candia. But by the abandonment of the five islands we should admit this claim, not only against ourselves, but against the Sultan, while wo should base our then anomalous reten tion of Corfu on the naked grounds that the islaud has a good harbour, is well fortified, and

that we want a commanding station in the Adriatic. Whether our moral position would be improved by such a proceeding it is for the country to determino. We have stated these objections to a plan which seems something like a foregone having offered himscli up for the conclusion in high quarters. But, like every one else, wo know we have a bad bargain in the Ionian Islands, and should Mr. Gladstone be able to settle their affairs on any satisfactory basis I10 will doubtless do himself much credit. But it certainly seems that Sir J. Young's desp; '1 obviates the necessity of any further nquiry by Mr. Gladstone or anybody c! \ The Lord Iligh Commissioner tells us all that can be told, þÿ that the Ionians are dissatisfied, and that, with short periods of lassitude, they keep up a perpetual exhibition of their discontent. He also makes it plain that the Constitution will not work, and that we must take one of three courses, þÿ cither to rule the Islands with a high hand, or to abandon them altogether, or to cut the useless ones adrift, and keep the military position of Curfu. What more than this Mr. Gladstone will be able to tell the House of Commons by next April it is difficult to imagine. The policy of Lord Derby in selecting so accomplished a man for the post of investigator is obvious enough ; lie makes a friend of Mr. Gladstone, and on this particular question he removes a portion of the responsibility of an important decision from his own shoulders. The Ministry will have Mr. Glad-

stone's voice for them in any measure which they may base on his report, while they will escape from the unwelcome task of first recommending a cession of territory, should such a plan be adopted. But the motive of Mr. Gladstone in accepting the appointment is difficult to trace. If it be public zeal, he is a good patriot, for he has ceatainly chosen an uninviting and invidious office. If, 011 the other hand, any political foresight prompts a temporary absence from Parliament or a well-timed service to a weak Govermcnt, then we must agree that his experience has already attained to a prophetic vision which we cannot rival.

The latest project of Walker and the filibusters to get up another expedition to Nicaragua lias been unceremoniously knocked on llie head by the action of the administration at Washington. It has been known for some time past as a matter of public news, and was officially brought under the cognizance of the national Executive, that tin expedition was being fitted out under t he lead and management of William Walker, and that the vessel, with the expeditionary army on board classed as peaceful emigrants, was to or clear from vvitli port of Mobile yesterday to-day, the the destination of San Juan del Norte. So long as the filibustering party furnished no stronger motives of interference than suspicion and public rumor, the government did not feel it its duty to interpose the strong arm of the law to prevent their departure ; but so soon as it had what appeared to it sufficiently strong grounds of action it did interpose, by issuing special orders to the collector at Mobile not to allow the expeditionary vessel to clear from that port. At the same time the collector was informed that in the case of persons wishing to go to Nicaragua as emigrants, and who were provided with the passports requird by the government of that republic, he was not to interfere with them, or to refuse the vessel conveying them a clearance. This new project of Walker's has been in course of preparation and maturing ever since his arrest at Punta Arenas by Commodore Paulding and his being sent back

to the United States. On that occasion he endeavoured to obtain sympathy and material aid here in New York, but was not very successful in that, and so he departed on a Southern tour, making speeches wherever he got an opportunity, and complaining bitterly of the action of Commo-

dore Paulding and the government in regard to him. In some of these speeches he made allegations implicating to a certain extent the President and some of the Cabinet in his adventures þÿ alleging, in fac;, that overtures had been made to him to turn his attention towards Mexico and filibusterizc it if lie chose, and that the government would not interfere with his operations there if lie would only let Nicaragua alone, as to which the government had designs of its own. These charges were noticed through the press, and awakened great surprise and much curiosity throughout the country. They were, of course, seini-officially denied ; whereupon Walker addressed a communication to the Mobile Register, under date of July 19, reiterating bis charges, and making them in the most formal ami unequivocal manner. We published the letter at the time, and now make the following extract from it : þÿ In the month of October last (1857) I was in New Orleans, preparing to return to Nicaragua. About the middle of the month G. neral lienningsen arrived from Washington, and soon after we met be informed ine that lie had important news to communicat e lie then pro lie ceeded to state that while in Washington had held several conversations with the Secretary of War; that in the course of one of the interviews the Secretary had informed him ot the determination on the part of the P esident to arrest the expedition to Nicaragua, adding at the same time that the acquisition of Cuba during his admini-tration was an object dear to

the heart of Mr. Buchanan. The Secretary further proceeded to say, according to General Hetiuingscn's report, that if we would turn our attention to Mexico and enter into the service of Comonfort, we should have the support ot the Uiited Stats government; that while in tlio Mexican s rvice we might by some act þÿ such as tearing down the flag of Spain þÿ bring about a war between Mi xico and Spain, and Cuba might then b srized by the lortner Power. The Seer, tary, according to the report I received, iutoruied General Heoningsen that means would not be lacking for such an enterprise, and when pressed liy the General to state how the means could he had, lie replied : " I have gone the length of my tether; before I can say m >ro it will be neccssaiy for tne to see a person above me." In tbe next interview the Secretary informed the General that be was not authorised to go further, but that ho> might iv ly iinp.icity on the menus being provided if the entei prise wcroundortnk n. When General Henningsen made this communication to me I was shocked at its nature, and rem-nked that the government could hardly he in earnest. To the Managers of sugar plantations in Christiausted's Jurisdiction. Mour. PEREGRINE PIROUETTE recently arrived from Paris, understanding that the education of many of been neglected in the graceful Art of Trip- the Gentlemen, here indicated, having in " youth ping it on the light fantastic toe," and being, as 1 am informed, influenced by the laudable desire, before too late, of acquiring that ease and gracefulness of movement, and carriage, without which no Gentleman can mingle in fashionable society with advantage, and which alone can be obtained by a proper proficiency in this delightful art, most respectfully begs leave to announce to all such as may be disposed to honor him, that as soon as he shall obtain a sufficient number of subscribers, he purposes opening a Daiiriiig Academy at the spacious saloon in the Ho'cl usually called Changement des Jambes where he will be most happy to give lessons in the above art on the most moderate terms. N. B. Those Gentlemen who may have previously acquired a knowledge of Dancing under the very ancient System þÿ a hi Irlandoir, vulgarly called " Sugane and Gad," will be charged only half price. I would earnestly wish to encourage Gentlemen not to be discourng d from coming forward iu order to avail themselves of this rare opportunity, because of the illiberal remarks made by proprietors regarding the numerous grand Routs given recently in succession by various Managers. Pay no attention to them ; it is all pure envy, nothing in

the world«but because they kuow they can not afford themselves to give such fine entertainments, where 30 to 40 Gentlemen and Ladies sit down to dinner, and afterwards dance all night þÿ but this just brings me to the point again cau Gentlemen dance if they don't know- þÿ how ? therefore now's your chance don't miss it. Suppose these routs, or parties, do keep the Labourers disturbed and up at night, produce confusion on the Estate, and the people arc thereby unable to go to work in the morning ; or $-ou, yourselves get a little " how come you sov and arc not able to attend to what the foolish Managers of the old School þÿ who used to make the large þÿCrops called their duty þÿ disregard all such fustian and console yourself with the reflection, that there's no use in Rum if no one will drink it ; and if you do sleep late, and feel muddled, and unfit for anything next day; sure, won't the Canes grow without your watching them ; and what's the use of an Overseer and a Driver if tlicy can't make the Labourers turn out in time to their work, and attend to other interests of the Estate ? þÿ I should like to know. And suppose Crops do fall short by your thus enjoying life, and when all comes to bo wound up at the close, proprietors or attorneys arc dissatisfied, what need you care ; dont you know how to

dance ? and can't you make up the deficient number of Hhds. sugar by an equal number of " l'eioucttes" or " Pigeon Wings j" an attorney or proprietor, I think, would be unreasonable indeed who would not be satisfied. Craving pardon for this digression Mons. PEREGRINE PEROUETTE has the further honor to announce his intention of giving also two grand entertainments weekly (days to be hereafter named) which, besides the usual practice in dancing, will comprise a variety of other amusements. The Drinkables will be abundant, and this department will be under the especial management of a Gentleman distinguished for his great prowess in this particular, and the number of Pupils he has brought forward in this line, and who, with just reason, boasts and prides himself 011 the number of bottles of wine which he put under his belt at a great drinking encounter, during his late travels, at a place called Kars ('the celebrated Fortress 1 suppose) wherein he came off Champion. This distinguished Gentleman, will also cacti of those evenings, amuse and astonish the company by his wonderful performances with the Learned rig which he has taught the wonderful art of whistling , and also to perform many other strange antics which can not fail to astound the audience. In fact he has, it is supposed, by long habit and association among these useful animals, obtained such wonderful power over them, (Rarey's power over lloises is a chicken to it) that many arc inclined to believe þÿ only it is

such a long time ago þÿ that lie (or, some one of his ancestors, may be,) must have entered a certain herd of these animals upon a memorable occasion, when tlicy all ran into the sea, aud therefore ever since he has retained this wonderful mastery. This Gentleman having lately increased his knowledge and greatly improved his moral feeling, will close each evening's entertainment by a Dissertation upon the lr niousness of Revenge and the want of Charity towards your neighbour, in which he will also icad an instructive lesson showing how prone men are to be disappointed in their aims when lured away by the gratification of these unhappy feelings, and how little faith, after all, there is to be placed in the promises of friends. PER EGR I N E P EROU ETT E.

CHRISTIANSTED, ST. CROIX. FRIDAY, 17tii DECEMBER, 1S58. þÿ þÿ The St. Thomas Times, in alluding to our remarks on the fine lately imposed 011 a lady for having brought a few letters in her trunk from New York, makt s the following sensible remarks : þÿ "We copy from our contemporary the Avis an article that relates a very summary proceeding with regard to a lady from New York, who we must suppose inadvertently had a few lctlers in her trunks intended to be distributed among friends, and had she seriously contemplated depriving the Post Office of its revenue, would too surely have sought other means of securing them than in her trunks, which she must have known were to he searched It would really seem that time nor silence serve to reconcile the public mind of these Islands in favor of the local Post Offices ; they continue to be held in the same dislike as when first established, and if they serve any purpose at all, it is only that they prove sources of the

ft f , ft & ft C X ft y j ft « exercise of occasional wit by the strange whose attention may be drawn to them. It is not long since we heard the Office compared to a carriage without wheels, a sleigh without horses, which, while they involuntarily oblige passengers to ride in them, are dependent upon auxiliary circumstances to provide the means of propulsion. It has also been compared to a onesided story, as there arc not two ends to its tale: i. e., it only engages to deliver letters within the King's Wharf and bug-hole, and has no return stage. It transmits only one way, the other folks may look out for themselves. Wc believe it is in the experience of all men, that Laws in every country, have in view, when ordained, even if at first stringent, the well being of the people, although it may restrain a few ; but the wisdom of the " Colonial Council of fcjt. Croix" in its Postal Law, has produced an abortion hideous to look at, and lias 110 countenance with any one, except its iuiuu ,'.iate nurses. Every doctor that has been called in to examine the case has given it as his opinion that the thing should be smothered. Now within ten years the wisdom of the same Council has given its aid to the making of very many Laws, that when come to be practically put to the test, have proved inoperative and illadapted to the customs long prevailing in the Islands þÿ and as you may convoy ten horses to a stream, yet not oblige one to drink þÿ so, in like way, the Laws proving repugnant every to one, if not abrogated, arc allowed to remain

dormant ; and of those the Postal Law is f ill ' as repugnant as any. Then why insist in forcing it ? Surely the Danish Colonies not the only places where laws have been 1> obsolete when not answering the object for which they were intended. Heaven knows, il the people of St. Croix need lilt their voices against the Postal Law, what must be our conditiou ! Let us for a moment suppose that the Post Office did possess utility, why even thou, the charge on letters would be cause of great objectiun. Just imagine four cents per half ounce to be paid for couveyiug a letter within the distance already alluded to, and without mentioning the number of persons that art pressed into its service without remuneration. For ourselves, we publish semi-annually a list of unclaimed letters extending from Alpha u Omega without right of charging a cent ! llut we arc not without confidence that those with whom the power lies will yet make the Postal Law a dead letter here." o THE INTEREST OF THE PRESS Till INTEREST OF THE PUBLIC. A practice has grown up lately which it, i very much the interest both of the press and the public should not become established aud inveterate. The allowing reports of proceedings in which the public have an interest to appear in the newspapers from day to day is very apt to bo looked upon as a favour done to the press at the expense of the dignity and propriety of a court, a commission, a meeting, or a legislative body. Thus, parliament for a long tiuie set itself against

the reporting of its debates, and those who did to our legislature this inestimable service relied upon its connivance, and were liable at any moment to punishment for breach of privilege. At last it has been discovered that the publication of debates was a groat deal more the affair of the public and the legislature than of the press; and it, was, in fact, a complete change in our constiþÿtution oneof those imperceptible adaptions which, far more than Reform Bills, have suited our old feudal machinery to meet the exigencies of modern times. So the presence of the press in our courts of justice has been found not mcro-

ly to be a benefit to newspapers, but a check and ass:stau-e of the most invaluable kind. The press secures to the administration of justice a real aud instantaneous pah. ty þÿ the best check to mal-administration, aud, by making the public parties to every step of a cause as it proceeds, has often called forth the most efficient assistance for the detection of guilt and the elucidation of truth. A short time since, and for a brief period, all the civilized world was ring . with the news of tl c successful termination oi i - great enterprise, and, in the presence of the gen ral rejoicing, men of science, if not agreed about the cable, were at least silent. Now, however, that the excitement and the cable have both died out, everything seems to have lapsed back into the same region of theory and speculation from which tno plan only emerged lor a short time to give a colour of plausibility to the opinions of all. We know not whether to account it as favourable to the cable or otherwise, but the fact remains that at the present moment most electiicians ol note agree to differ both as to the nature and extent ol injury to the wire and the chances of its ever being again restored to working order. One thing, however, seems to admit of no doubt, and that is, that, contrary to all expectation, it shows no signs of becoming worse. In the presence of this encouraging fact there are many eminent in science who believe, first, that the injuries to its insulation exist much nearer the Irish shore than was at first supposed ; and, secondly, that by using different instruments the whole line may be, to a certain extent, used for the transmission of messages, if not from > country to America, at least from America igland. The means used for testing cab t > a certain the spot at which an injury has occu .1 are always so far unsatisfactory that, uuder the best circumstances, the result only affords a negative proof. Thus,

when it is stated that the defect is supposed to exist at about 300 miles from the Irish coast, it means nothing more than that the damage does not extend beyond that distance, though it by no means proves that the injury may not bo within as 20 or 30 miles om shore. The test, in fact, hall the length we have stated, or even so near . means that alter escaping the injured portion of the cable only sufficient electricity is let t to pass along the conductor for about 300 miles, and that at that d' nee the resistance to the current is equal to a total rupture of the wire, or " dead earth'' as it is technically called. All practical electricians, however, admit that the injuries may and very likely do exist within a distance of 50 ro'Ies from land, and that these consist not of one but many slight losses of insulation, with very likely partial separation of the conductor at parts where the two-mile lengths were originally joined That the damage cannot exist as far out as 300 miles is almost evidenced by the fact of the receipt of the American messages long after nouc could bo sent from this side of the Atlantic. It may appear strange to some of our readers that the wire which conveys the signa.s to this country is not sufficiently intact to a'low of the transmission of answers through the same medium. A moment's reflection, however, will show that the injuvies to the c .ble, being near the land, allow so much of the electric current to escape that what remains is not sufficient to

overcome the resistance of tlio wire for more than a short portion of its entire length. With currents from the New World, on the contrary, the electric wave, as it is called, of a signal comes along the wire intact till near our shores. Here, though much of it escapes, sufficient is h it, nevertheless, to mark some signals at Val. utia, þÿ weakly and variably, it is true, but still occasionally enough to form letters, though, from causes which we shall presently endeavour i show, it is impossible now to render them iuto intelligible words TTp to within the last few days the shore end at Valcntia has been the ordinary deep-sea portion of the cable, made, as our readers are aware, of the very lightest form consistent with the strcugth necessary for its being safely submerged. That such a wire, within the wash of the Atlantic waves, and lying in some parts over a very rocky bottom, must have sustained injury seems at first sight inevitable. This portion is now bciug replaced by i be proper shore-ends, which are of strength and hi .'less sufficient to withstand any tide. Up to he present the length which has been undo i in order to substitute the shore end has, strange to say, been found uninjured, though it is not expected that this will prove the case when the whole 12 miles shall have been recovered and replaced with the stout cable. It is, of course, looked upon as certain that laying down the shore end must improve the conditiou of the whole cable ; else, of course, the expense and labour of submerging it

s T -. 0 b o ( « ay ( would never be attempted. Even in its present state the signals received at Valentia are occasionally as distinct as those of some overland wires, and should any improvement take place when the shore end is added on, there are many who profess themselves confident of working through the whole wire for some time to come at 1< ;'st. Foremost among those who express this opinion is Professor Hughes, whose printing telegraph is extensively used in the United States, and which will also in the course of a few weeks more bo introduced into Australia to work through the first submarine telegraph of that colony between Tasmania ud Melbourne. Mr. Hughes states himself confident of being able even now to signal through the Atlantic cable, and is anxious to conduct all his experiments upon the wire at his own expense. The Atlantic Telegraph Company, on the other hand, say they have no disinclination to permit Mr. Hughes to try his skill ; yet, strange to say, though both parties are willing, nothing is done nevertheless. Now, however, that the matter is made public Mr. Hughes may feel bound to press his offer, and the Atlantic Company, in fairness and in duty to its shareholders, will perhaps see the necessity of at once accepting a liberal proposal, which, whichever way it results, can do them or their cable no mauner of injury, but, on the other hand, may possibly be of immense benefit. It will very likely be interesting to many of our readers if we explain at once on what grounds Mr. Hughes rests his hope ol'makiug the delunct

wire speak again, especially as by so doing wc may be able to point out the general nature of t ie difficulties which have gradually made the sigu ds from the other side of the Atlantic unintelligible. When the first unsuccessful attempt was made to lay the wire, it will be recollected that it parted from under the Niagara's stern at some 350 miles distance from the Irish coast. The piece thus submerged remaiued, of course, attached to the shore end for a considerable period, and then, for the first time, the phenomenon of " magnetic storms, or, as they are now called, eartli currents," was observed. Of the causes of these earth currents, or tlio laws by which they are governed, nothing is yet known. They may be briefly described as irregular currents of electricity passing through the outer wire covering of the cable, and which, according to the laws of induced currents, create auother currcut in the conductor of the cable itself, funning in a contrary direction to that in which the earth current travels along the outside. The effect of these on the conductor was, of course, to deflect rapidly the needle of the galvanometer to which it, was attached, precisely as it signals were being sent quickly. Sometimes these earth currets were so violent as to cause the ne die to vibrate with such rapidity that it was impossible to follow its movements with the eye. Singular enough, these storm currents were always at their worst at 10 o'clock at night and 10 in the morning, while they were, on the

other hand, always least, felt at 1 1 o'clock in the morning and 11 at night. Beyond these general facts nothing seems to have beeu known about them. When the cable was laid last August the instruments were on the principle of Morse's recording telegraph, according to the system of which three or lour currents or signals sent across the Atlantic arc necessary to form one letle.r of a word. While the cable was in good ord r, and its insulation tolerably perfect, tliis pla , worked well enough, its greatest and most us drawback only being that the method s a very slow one, since on the average fuur uais were required to one letter, and five letto is oil the average went to one word. However, all went well until the fast increasing defective insulation of the wire became mauifest, and the earth currents began to take a most unpleasant part in the telegraphing. As the electric current of the signals lost force nearing the Irish shore the earth currents overpowered them, and in the middle of the letter made one or more ui. intelligible signs, the task of reading became more and more difficult, till, with the increasing derangement of the line, consecutive words gradually ceased, and at last even le tters eamo only at rare intervals. Comparatively speaking this difficulty was not experienced on this side of the Atlantic till, for tin reasons wc have stated, it had long overcome the messages to America; and to this reason it is owing that even the first signals sent from hero wore con-
stantly answered " from Newfoundland with "Repeat'' and Send slower." So much for

the stoppage of the wire. The reason for Mr. Hughes's confident belief of being able now to work through simply arises from the fact that his instrument þÿ the printing telegraph þÿ is not exposed to anything like the same amount of risk from earth currents. His instrument is, on a small scale, on very much the bamc principle as to shape and plan as Mr. Hoe's American printing machine. It is worked by means of key-notes, like those of a small piano, each key being marked with the letters of the alphabet. Thus, touching a key at one end of the wire transmits a current to the other, where, instead of the paper, as in Morse's telegraph, receiving a dint or mark that forms part of a letter, the entire letter itself is printed. The advantage of this is obvious. One current suffices to form one letter instantaneously, instead of four or five currents. Less time is thus given for the action of earth currents; or, even in case of their acting and printing in some cases other letters than those sent, it by no means follows that the letteis so misplaced would prevent, the accurate meaning of the sentence being read. Allow that under the worst circumstances one-fourth of the letters, owing to the action of the earth currents were wrong, sufficient would be right and sufficicDlly consecutive to permit the tncuuing of the whole to be lively read. At all events, Mr. Hughes's machine utilizes the currents to their utmost, since he makes one suffice for clearly printing one letter, instead of requiring three or

four. The only doubt is, can two such complicated machines be made to work with mathema- 'ieal accuracy when 3,000 miles apart? This "1'jection is urged as something almost insuperable, though noue deny that it is purely a mechanical one, and one that, can be overcome. So far, however, are we from considering it insuperable that we think a very simple process would remedy it if' practically such an obstacle is found to exist, vvnich we by no means deny might he the case. Both the machines at Newfoundland and Valentia would have to be made with the accuracy of chronometers, it being understood that both are to be put biek to a given zero when a message wis either sent or received. Let the first current then sent for a message either way liberate and set l oth instruments in motion, precisely in the same way as the letter is now printed, by liberating tbe armature and pressing iho paper against the little wheel of typo. The proper working of the machine is, however, Mr. Hughes's affair. It is only his offer to the Atlantic Company with which we have to deal, and whether it is woitli anything or nothing should be decided by actual test, and the sooner the better. As the matter stands at present he lias made his offer and it lias not been declined, and so I lie thing re.-ts, like a child's rocking-horse, moving without advancing.

From the Weekly Despatch, October 31 Prosecution of Count Montalembert.

Paris, Friday MorniDg. The Moniteur announce that the Correspondent has been seized for an article by Count Montalembert upon England and India. A prosecution is to be instituted agaiust Count Montalembert and the publisher of t he periodical. The publisher and author of this article are accused of attacks against the principle of universal suffrage, the right of authority which the Emperor is invested with by tho Constitution, and the respect due to the laws. They are further charged with attempting to excite the people to hatred and contempt of Government, and endeavouring to disturb the public peace. The article is headed þÿ England and þÿIndia, aud Count Montalembert, though þÿ giving vent to the just indignation so properly excited by the excessive severity of the punishments which the English intiict on the conquered insurgents and þÿprisoners, pays some very high compliments to our free institutions, drawing very 1 unfavourable comparisons with France. We presume the following passages arc among those objected to : þÿ þÿ When 1 find my fit of it coming on, when my ears arc dinned sometimes with the buzz of the antechamber chroniclers, sometimes with the clamour of fanatics who believe themselves to he our masters, and of hypocrites who fancy us their dupes ; when 1 feel stifled beneath the weight of an atmosphere loaded with servile and corrupting effluvia, 1 hasten away to breathe, a purer air, and take a life-bath in free England I came forth from this august

spectacle (a Parliamentary debate on India) full of emotion as might any man who looks to a Government as something above a þÿlacquey s waiting-room, and who seeks in a civilised nation something better than a fl ick of sheep only fit for the shears, or to be led to nibble in silence under the shadow of an enervating security It would be the acme of unreason and injustice were we to regard England as the only guilty nation, or as the guiltiest among the nations of the earth. Her policy is neither more egotistical nor more immoral than that of other great States of ancient and modern history. 1 believe it would even bo possible to prove a thesis just the reverse. It is not charity, but well-ordered justice, that begins at home, and upon this ground no French publicist has a right to fall foul of þÿEngland p s olicy before be lias stated his opinion of tho crimes committed by French policy during the Revolution and the Empire, and not such as its adversaries represent it, but such as its apologists describe it þÿ M. Thiers, for instance. You may search among the. most suspected dark corners of English diplomacy, but in vain, for you will find nothing there to resemble, even remotely, tho destruction of the Republio of Venice or tho murderous ambuscades at Bayonne. . . Returning to France I find in L' Univers, 23rd of May, 1858, Parliamentary Government styled a farce, wiih scenic decorations Happy country and happy clergy, whose organ gives such sound information in
such decorous phraseology . Scribes who interlard visions of the Virgin with scurrilous invectives against the grandeur of Great þÿBritain.

The political dissentions that prevailed for a twelve-month past ill the Dominican Republic have happily terminated. The treasonable dc- I ing copy of a report furnished to Ilis Excellency signs, the abuse of power, and the private speculations alleged against the Ex-President Baez, were provocations that a free people in the enjoyment of their indisputable rights, could never j Tuesday evening. The investigation into the tolerate for an hour. Their unanimous and decided action which hurled him from power, that invested him in the city the only foothold that he retained, until he was compelled to surrender, arc events we shall not now recur to. This being accomplished, the nation þÿ þÿmasse proclaimed their able and faithful countryman General Santana as Chief of the State, with full powers to reorganise its institutions ; and the profouud repose, order, and tranquility which the country has since enjoyed, present a complete guarantee for the general satisfaction that prevails. This state of matters, however, has been scandalously invaded of late by the appearance there of Mr. Maximo Ray baud, late Consul General of France to Hayti. Desirous apparently of turning to some personal advantage the late political complications which were combined with the unfortunate occurrence of a failure of the crops, M. liaybaud lias been accused of endeavoring to spread a propaganda in favor of the Emperor Soulouque. It is even said, he had the effrontery to address a document to General Santana containing the grossest
misrepresentations, and the most offensive strictures upon the state of the Republic ; with strong insinuations that it was his duty and his

S tr. & B 0 Ij a V; ll s. interest to submerge his country again in the iron grasp of Haytien despotism. Such a gratuitous insult was promptly responded to by sending the gentleman his passport, with a recommendation to avail himself of it, at the earliest opportunity. This singular mission of M. Raybaud lias naturally given rise to numerous conjectures. In his note to General Santana, it is alleged, that he threatens fresh invasions by the Emperor Soulouque, exposes the impoverished state of the Republic, refers to the danger and impolicy of American connections, and exaggerates the exhausted condition of the population. As an example of the impoverished state of the Republic, tlio entire public debt exists in the form of a circulating paper currency, which might bo cancelled for less than $300,000, and all the international claims that | ossibly might be trumped up, arising from incidents over which the present Administration could have no control, do not exceed $200,000 more. These are all the responsibilites of the Republic, whose area embraces, without exception, one of the richest and productive regions of the globe ; responsibilities which two years of economy alone, could effectually discharge. As for the exhausted condition of the inhabitants, they never were in better fighting order and spirit, which His Imperial Majesty will doubtless soon have another taste of, decisively so, should the occasion be provoked ; and lie may rest assured, that as long as a potato can grow upon the soil, and a pound of gunpowder

is to be procured, Dominican valor and patriotism will never succumb to Haytien force of arms. There is no doubt, that the important bay of Santana plays an interesting part in all these intrigues ; but it is high time the Dominican question with Hayti, should bo definitely settled. The leading question, affecting as it does most intimately the great and material interests of the country, is Immigration It is a question that has been sadly neglected for many years past. Neither Sir Charles Grey, nor Sir Henry Barkly appeared to draw its importance in tlio light in which they who knew the relative slate of population to agriculture have for many years considered it. Preservation of ttie þÿDead. M. Falcon)', a French chemist, has patented a process for preserving and embalming dead bodies. On Tuesday he exhibited the results to a number of gentlemen in the lecture-luiU of the School of Medicine, Orosvenor-place. M. Falcony uses a powder, composed chiefly of a neutral salt, mixed with sawdust, which obsorbs moisture, and so combines with the most deadly exhalations that no injury can be sustained by persons being brought into the closest contact with the deceased ; and, by preventing putrefaction for more than a fortnight, will enable families to be brought together from distant places in time for the interment. In large cities the possibility of contagion when people have died oi fevers or cholera will he avoided, as by the use of the powder the body is dried up, and after a time falls into dust. The process for embalming is by means of a liquid which appears to answer its purpose ; but in this the public will feel less interest than in the temporary preservation of bodies to prevent injury to the health of the living.

When the last Packet Steamer left Southampton the Atrato had already arrived with the homeward Mails and we may consequently expect that she will bring out the Mails due on the 2nd next. We have no local news to record. The Burgher Council, we are informed, is occupying itself with the Immigration Question. With the results arrived at, we do not expect to be informed for some time yet. Whether, however, such an impoitant matter should lie settled without being openly and thoroughly discussed, is a questiun which few could bo prepared to answer in the affirmative. We are not acquainted with all the bearings of the question ; (for how should we be, in fac3 of the secret-system carried on around us) but yet we dare venture to assert, that the existing labouract, in its application to our present labourers and those expected to immigrate to this Island, is fraught with a good deal of serious speculation ; and, consequently, no decision ought to ho arrived at, without giving the subject such a degree of publicity as will ensure a a thorough discussion of the question.

ST. PETERSBURG, AND ITS PALACES. Correspondence of The N. Y. Tribune. St. Petersburg, July, 1858. No two cities can be more unlike than Moscow and St. Petersburg; they scarcely appear to have been built by the same people. Were it not for some of the older churches, which seem curiously out of place here, a traveler coining from the former city, would imagine that he had already left Russia. The strange, fantastic, picturesque, Tartar character has disappeared, and all that one sees is suggestive of Western Europe. This is but the first impression, however. The second is that of a power so colossal as to coerce Nature herself-þÿ a power which can only he developed when unbounded resources are placed under the direction of a single will þÿ and herein wc again recognize Russia. St. Petersburg is also a marvel in its way, and if the interest which it excites is of a totally different character from that which one feels in Moscow, it is no less imposing and permanent. No man except Peter the Great would have conceived the idea of building a city here. Yet, if we leave out of sight the physical difficulties against which lie had to contend, and consider not only the character of his ambition, but the inadequateness of any other site on the Baltic coast to meet its designs, wc cannot sec that lie could liavo done otherwise. Had ho selected Nijni Novgorod, as he first intended, the heart of Russian power would have been placed on the borders of Asia, still further from the influence of European civilization. Russia,

in this case, would never have attained to a first place in the councils of European nations. It lvas necessary to approach the west. Finland and Livonia were at that time in ie possession of Sweden, and Poland was still nation. Peþÿter s choice, therefore, was restricted to the shores of the Gulf of Finland. Here, truly, ho might found other sites presenting fewer natural obstacles, but at the same time fewer natural advantages. The Neva, through which the largest lake in Europe pours its waters into the sea, afforded a ready-made communication, not only with Novgorod and Onega, but with a

S Tv C R 0 lj t A, V I $ large portion of tlat Finland whose acquisition he even then fore, aw, while the island of Cronstadt, guarding tie entrance from the Gulf, offered a fitting station for his infant navy. The extreme high latitude of the new Capital was even an adviutage. Winter was his ally then, as it has hem the best ally of Russia in the later times. And the wisdom of his selection lias just again been demonstrated, when the combined naval strength of Europe lay before Cronstadt and did not dare to attack it. But nothing slio.-t of that genius, which is the same thing as madness in tho eyes of the world, would have undertaken the work. Here where the Neva, a broad, full, rapid stream, spreads itself out among swampy islands, completely flooding them whe:i the Spring freshets have burst the ice, and win re a strong south-west wind drives the waters of the Gulf high over tho highest land the city stands upon, have arisen clusters of g:gantic edifices, mountains of masonry, in their solid durability bidding defiance to the unstable soil. The marshy shores of the river are hidden under league-long quays of massive granite ; millions of piles bear aloft the tremendous weight of palaces, churches, obelisk ml bridges ; and four grand canals, p issing ihia ugh and around the city, so tap the Neva of Ills aen icing strength that the fearful inundations of former years cannot be repeated. Oue hundred and iifiy years have passed away since Peter built his cottage in the midst of an uninhabited wilderness, and now there stands

on the spot one of the first of European capitals, with a population of more than half a million. The town was first commenced on the northern bank of the Neva, on the Aptekarskoi, or þÿApothecary I s sland. In cold climates, a man always builds his house fronting the south. Very soon, however, the southern bank received the preference, on account of its convenience and its proximity to a little rising ground. At present three-quarters of the city, if not more, are south of the Neva, the remaining portion being scattered over the two large islands of Aptekarskoi and Vassili Ostrov. Those who know Berlin, can form a tolerable idea of those parts of St Petersburg distant from the liver. The streets are alike broad and regular, the houses high, massive and plain. But there is not the Kttinon.m anil tameness of the Prussian capital. Even now, when the Court is absent, the fashionable world off on its travels, and nobody at home, it is as lively a city as one could ( well wish to see. Five thousand droshkies and as many carriages rattle hither and thither from morning till night þÿ or rather, continuously, for you can see to read in the streets at midnight, and they are then by no means deserted. þÿAY here the summer is so fleeting it is doubly enjoyed, and during these long, delicious twilights, especially, no one remains in-doors who can get out. The approach to the city from the land side is particularly tame. On such a dead level the first block of buildings shuts out the view of

everything beyond, and even when you roach the JYevskvi Prospekt þÿ Petersburg þÿ and look down its vista of three the Broadway of St. miles, the only thing you see is the gilded spire of the Admiralty Buildiug, at the end. On
enough to copy and carry away in your mind. Proceeding down the Nevskoi Prospckt to this

thing is large, substantial and imposing, but nothing more. Even the Annitshkoff Palace, which you see on the right, as you approach the Fontanka Canal, docs not particularly impress you. The bridge over the canal, however, demands more than a passing glance. At each end arc two groups in bronze by a Rus- ' sian sculptor, whose name I am sorry not to know. They arc called the IIorsc-Tarners,

a violent struggle for the mastership. The style of taming has no resemblance whatever to Mr. þÿRarey s, but the figures are very bold and spirited. The Emperor Nicholas presented copies of two of these groups to the King of Prussia, who placed them on the comers of the Museum front, in Berlin, where they have been christened by the people, þÿ Progress Preventþÿed and þÿ Reaction þÿEncouraged. Continuing our course down the Novskoi Prospekt, we pass iu succession, on the right, the Alexander Theater, the Gostinnoi Dvor

or Great Bazaar, and the Cathedral of Our Lady of Kazan. The latter is built of gray Finland granite, with a circular colonnade in front, copied from that of St. þÿPeter at s Rome. In the open space inclosed by the colonnade are bronze statues of Kutusoff and Barclay do Tolly. The buildings on either hand become more lofty and imposing, the throng in the street greater, and soon after crossing tho last of tho canals, the Moika, we enter the famous Admiralty Square þÿ the grand center of St. Petersburg, around which are grouped its most impotant buildings and monuments Here everything is on such a grand scale, that the magnitude of the different objects is at first not apparent to the eye, The Square is about a mile iu length, by a quarter of a mile in breadth. In front of us is the Admiralty Building, with a front of 1,500 Let, and wings resting on the Neva, G50 feet in length. To the right of it is the YVinter Palace, with 700 feet front, and still further the Hermitage, nearly as large. Opposite these two is the Hotel de þÿl Etat Major, of corresponding proportions, while the Alexander Column þÿ a monolith of red granite, þÿ 160 feet in height, including pedestal and capital rises from the center of the square between. Turning to the left, we see the huge golden dome of the þÿIzak s Cathedral, lifted between three and four hundred feet into the air, and gleaming like a fallen sun on the summit of a granite mountain. The western end of the great square is taken up by the Synod and

Senate Houses, whose fronts are united in one long facade by a sort of trium, bal arch. Between them and the Admiralty, on 1 he bank of the Neva, is the celebrated equestrian statue of Peter the Great. Here are the elements of an architectural panorama of the giaudest kind, jet the general effect is þÿbj no means such as one would anticipate, and simply because one indispensable condition has been overlooked þÿ proportion. With the exception of the þÿIzaak Cathedral, s there is not a single edifice iu this square which is not much too low for the extent of its base. Hence, they all appear to be lower than is really the fact, and as they arc of very nearly uniform height, the eye ranges around the squares, seeking in vain for some picturesque break in the splendid monotony. A skilful architect might have at least iniiigated this fault, but those who planned the Admiralty and the Winter Palace seetn to have been even incapable of perceiving it. The latter building is quite disfigured by the placing of a sort of half-story above the true cornice. < hi tinother hand, the þÿIzaak Cathedral, s of which 1 shall have more to say hereafter, is one of t lnvcry finest specimens of modern architecture in existence. It stands in the center of a small square of its own, opening into that of the Admiralty at its western end ; and here, decidedly, is the most striking view of St. Petersburg. On one side is the Cathedral, on the other the Neva, against whose sparkling current and the long line

of buildings ou his northern hank gallops Peter on his huge block of granite ; while far iu front of the Alexander Column, soaring high above, the surrounding buildings, is seen in its true proportion. Crossing the Square, between the Admiralty the Neva, only, and the Admiralty Square, j Building and the Winter Palace, we stand upon can you get anything like a picture broad | the bank of the Neva. Directly opposite opens the main brunch , or little Neva, dividing Vassili Ostrov and the Aptekarskoi Islands. The river central point, you arc not particularly struck i is here more than a third of a mile in breadth, of with the architecture on either hand. Every- | a clear, pale green color, and rapid current. At the intersection of the two arms, on Vassili Ostrov, stands the Exchange, a square building with a Grecian facade. To the left of it is the long front of the Academy of Sciences, then the Academy of Arts, and at the extremity of our view, when the main branch of the Nova turns northward into the Gulf of Finland, the School of Miuos. In front of the Aptekarskoi, and separated from it only by a moat, is the old each representing a man and horse, engaged in | fortress of Peter and Paul, now a prison lor nobles, with the tall-spircd church, in the vaults of which rest Peter the Great and all the monarchs since his time. On the southern bank, ou which wc stand, a row of palaces stretches away on our right to the Trinity Bridge, beyond which we see tho green linden-trees of the

Summer gardens. From cither shore of the river, or from the bridges which span it, the pictures are always broad, bright and cheerful. Splendid granite stairways lead down to the water, gayly-painted boats dart to and fro, little steamers keep up a communication with tho further islands, and the miles of massive quay on

either side are thronged with a busy populace. Hero the midsummer heat is always tempered by a delightful breeze, and the very sight of the dancing water is cooling, under this pale, hot, quiet sky. I do not wonder at the enthusiasm of the St. Petersburgers for the Neva. Its water is so remarkably soft and sweet that they prefer it to all other water in the world. The Emperor Alexander always carried a supply with him, bottled, when ho was absent from the eipital. The stranger, however, cannot drink it with impunity, as its effect on an unaccustomed bo ly is medical in the highest degree. The Winter Palace stands upon the site of the old one, which was destroyed by fire in 1837. þÿKohl account s of this latter structure is worth j quoting. The suits of apartments were perfect household, labyrinths, who and even the chief of the Imperial had filled that post for twelve years, was not perfectly acquainted with all the forests of great landholders, many colonies arc nooks and corners of the building. As in the j I settled of which the owner takes no notice, so there nestled many a oue in this palace not included among the regular inhabitants. For example, the watchmen on the roof, placed there for different purposes, among others to keep the water in the tanks from freezing during the Winter, by casting in red-hot balls, built themselves huts between the chimneys, took their wives and children there, nud even kept poultry and goats, which fed on the grass of the roof: it is sai l that at last some crows were introduced,

but this abuse bad been corrected before the palace was þÿburnt, Fortunately, the new palace is not so labyrinthine, though of equal extent. During the residence of Nicholas there, 0,000 persons frequently lived in it at one time. Strang rs are freely allowed to visit all parts of it, on presenting a ticket, which the major-domo gives mi application. Formerly, the visitor was I obliged to appear in full dress, hut in the general relaxation of laws and customs which has followed the accession of Alexander II , this rule has also been given up. Our Minister, Mr. Seym iur, also informed mo that the Emperor rc- < ives American citizens in ordinary civil dress, n it requiring them to appear in Court costume. There is no other Court in Europe which, with such immense moans and such magnificent appointments, preserves so great a simplicity. Toe free-lorn from ostentation or parade in the l n,i -rial family of Russia, except upon stated oe o-i iih, is a very agreeable feature. Nowhere e s 1 does the monarch walk about his capital, no ittended. The Empress, even, may take a l stroll, if she likes. We met oue day the C:uretitch. or Crown Prince, with two of his younger brothers, in a plain two-horse carriage with a siuglo soldier as footman. Those fine, fresh, handsome boys were quite alone, and looked as if they were competent to take care of themselves. The grandfather of the reigning Empress was a Stallmcister (Master of the Horse) in Darmstadt, and she is probably indebted to him

for her prudent, amiable, sensible character. Nicholas was aware of her descent, but be wisely gave bis sons perfect freedom to choose their own wives, and welcomed her as cordially as if her ancestry dated from Julius C®sar. Iu visitiug the palace, I was particularly struck with the cheerful plainess of the private apartments, which contrasted remarkably with the pomp and dazzle of those for state occasions. To describe minutely all that I saw in the Winter Palace would take up several chapters. Wo were between two and three hours in walking slowly through the principal balls and chambers. A large number of these are devoted to pictures, principally portraits and battle scenes. A large room contains several hundred portraits of the officers who served against Napoleon in 1813-14. Then follows the Hail of the Marshals, with few and full-length figures, some of which are of groat historical interest. Potemkin is here represented iu full armor, a tall, Apollonian figure, over six feet in height, with a fine oval head, regular and handsome features, soft blue eyes, and curly golden hair Suwarrow is a short man, with a largo benevolent head, very broad in the temples, whore phrenologists place the orgin of oonstruetiveness. He wears a plain leather jacket and breeches, and resembles nothing so much as an old Quaker preacher. Barclay de Tolly is tall, slender, stern and thoughtful, with a prematurely bald head: Kutusoff short, thick, coarse and heavy-featured. In striking contrast with these personages is Wellington,
with his cold, prim English face and small head.

s T. 0 fl 0 I X A V I) S , The battle-pieces represent all the noted fields in which Russian arms have been engaged, from Narva to Inkerniann þÿ not merely an ostentatious display of victories, but important defeats as well, so that the series presents a true historical interest. Narva receives as prominent a place as Pultava, Borodino as Leipzig, Silistria as Ismail. Many ol the later pictures are fine works of art : the illustrations of the Persian and Circassian wars, especially, are full of rich dramatic effect. Altogether, this gallery will compare very well "with that of Versailles. One of the most inteiesting halls is that devoted to the coronation gifts received by Alexander, Nicholas and the present Emperor. The ancient custom is still preserved, of each province throughout the Empire sending bread and salt as a token of welcome. But the loaf is carried upon a massive salver of gold and silver, of the rarest workmanship, and the salt iu a box or cup of the same material, studded with jewels. The salvers presented to the two former Emperors rise in dazzling pyramids from the floor nearly to the ceiling, but they are far outshone by those of Alexander IF., who received just as much as his father and uncle together. If the wealth lavished upon these offerings is an index to the popular feeling, it is a happy omen for his reign. The taste, richness and variety of the ornaments bestowed upon the mighty golden salvers exceeds anything of the kind I ever saw. Their value can only be estimated by millions. It is signi-

ficant, perhaps, that the largest and most superb, which occupies the place of honor, in the center of the glorious pile, is the offering of the soils of the Imperial domains. We were admitted into the room containing the crown jeweds, which arc arranged iu glass cases, according to their character and value. Iu the center is the crown of Alexander, a hemisphere of the purest diamonds : beside is the scepter, containing the famous brilliant purchased by Cathrine II. from a Greek slave, and for a time supposed to be the largest in the world It turns out to be smaller than the Koh-i-nor, though (to my eyes, at least,) of a purer water. 'There is not a quarter so many jewels here as in the Treasury at Moscow, yet their value far exceeds that of the latter. The stones are ol the largest and rarest kind, and the splendor of their tints is a delicious intoxication to the eye. The soul of all the fiery roses of Persia lives in these rubies; the freshness of all velvet sward, whether iu Alpine valley or English lawn, in these emeralds; the bloom of southern seas in these sapphires, and the essence of a thousand harvest moons in these necklaces of pearl. Before leaving the Palace we were conducted to a small room iu the first story, in the northwestern corner. Two Imperial guardsmen stood at the door, and two old servants in livery were in a little anteroom, ouo of whom accompanied us into the narrow chamber where Nicholas lived and died. Nothing lias been changed since his body was carried out of it. The bard camp-bed

(so small aud narrow that I should not wish to sleep upon it) stands there, beside bis writingtable. On a stool at the foot lies bis dressinggown. His comb, brushes, gloves, pocketliandkcrchief, knife and pencil arc carelessly laid upon a small toilet-table, under a very moderatesized looking-glass. A plain green carpet covers the floor, and the half-dozen chairs are liued with green leather. The walls arc almost concealed by pictures, either landscapes or battle-pieces, and few of them of any value. Just over his pillow is a picture of a very pretty young girl, dressed as a soldier. It is scarcely possible to believe that the occupant of this room has been dead for more than three ye irs. Every object suggests life, and while we arc examining them we half expect to see that colossal figure, which all Europe knew so well, appear at the door. The only thing which has been added is a very beautiful drawing of the þÿEmperor head, s after death. The expression upon the face is that of pain and trouble, not the serene, impenetrable calm whieh it wore during life. The Hermitage, adjoining the Winter Palace, was built by Catharine, as a place of escape from the fatigue of Court ceremonials, and of quiet conversation with a few privileged persons. The name seems to have been jestingly, or ironically given. Who would not be a hermit in this immense pile, whose walls are of marble, blazing with gold, whose floors of the choicest inlaid woods, and whose furniture the rarest and most
costly workmanship in porphyry, jasper, lapiz-

laguli and malachite ? Such splendor is not now out of place, since the palace has been given up to the Arts. The vast collection of pictures accumulated by the Russian Etnperors is here displayed, together with a gallery of sculpture, one of the finest assortments of antique gems in tho world, a collection ol Grecian and Etruscan antiquities, and a library of rare books aud manuscripts. The picture gallery is particularly rich in the works of Reubens, Vandyke, Rembrandt, Murillo, and the Dutch school, and though it contains few celebrated master-pieces, tho number of really good pictures is remarkable.
