FRANCE. THE EMPEROR NAPOLEON ON THE "FREE LABOUR" SCHEME. The Moniteur of Sunday publishes the following letter from the Emperor : þÿ To Prince Napoleon, Minister of Algeria and the Colonies. St. Cloud, Oct. 30, 185S. that at the moment when the difference witli My þÿ dear Cousin, þÿ I have the liveliest desire Portugal, relative to the Charles-Georges, has terminated þÿ the question of the engagement of free labourers ou the African coast should be definitely examined and finally settled on the truest principles of humanity and justice. I energetically claimed from Poitugai the restitution of the Charles-Georges, because I will always maintain intact the independence of the national flag; hut, in this case even, it was only with the profound conviction of my right that I risked with the King of Portugal a rupture of those friendly relations which 1 am glad to maintain with him. But as to the principle of the engagement of the negroes, my ideas arc far from being settled. If, in truth, labourers recruited on the African coast are not allowed the exercise of their free will, and if this enrolment is only the Slave-trade in disguise, I will allow it on no terras ; for it is not I who will any where protect enterprises contrary to progress, to humanity, and to civilisation. I bag you then to seek out the truth with the zeal and intelligence which you bring to hear on all affairs about which you employ yourself. And as the best method of putting a term to what is a continual cause of

dispute would be to substitute the free labour of Indian coolies for that of the negroes, I beg you to come to an understanding with the Minister lor Foreign Affairs to resume with the English Government the negotiations which were entered upon a few mouths ago. On this, my dear cousin, I pray God to have you in his holy keeping. NaPoLeoX. The Pays and Prcssc, which so flatly denied any intention of abandoning the "free immigration scheme," have already changed their tactics in consequence of the Imperial letter. The Presst says : þÿ " A question of some importance deserves indeed to be thoroughly examined. We ourselves have already insisted upon the necessity of an investigation. The debate is now open, and the question will be discussed in the light of day, for both the foreign and French press will be eager to take part in au inquiry iu which all maritime nations and civilisation itself are deeply interested." According to the construction put upon the Emperor's letter by the Nord of Brussels, the French Government only intends to renounce the traffic in African blacks on condition that it shall obtain from England all the facilities desired for the substitution of Coolies. If this be true, Prince Napoleon is ordered to inquire into one set of facts, while the conclusion to which he is to come will be governed by another. If Coolies can he had in sufficient number, the African scheme will be pronounced analogous to the Slave-trade, but otherwise it will be said to and " France will not sacrifice her colonies to be nothing like it because labour must be had,

England." The Nord further affirms that the Emperor's offer places the English Government " it remains difficulty," in a "cruel to he seeu whether the Ministers and it snceringly says, will be more accommodating with regard to Hindoos than they were when the former negotiations were broken off." The funeral car of Napoleon I. arrived on Friday morning iu Paris. General Sir J. Burgoyne, charged by the Queen of England to proceed with it to the Invalidcs and deliver it up formally, was iu attendance. At a quarter before 1 o'clock General Count d'Ornano, the Governor, and his staff, descended into the courtyard to meet Marshal Vaillant, Minister of War. In a few minutes after the English General and Prince Napoleon, who had come from Compiegnc expressly for the occasion, arrived, and the ceremony of reception took place in front of the church, where the car had been address: þÿ placed. Sir " J. Bargoyne delivered the following Her Majesty the Queen of England, being desirous of offering to his Imperial Majesty a rclio which she knows to be interesting to France, has charged me to bring to Paris, and to place at the disposal of the Emperor, the

funeral car on which were conveyed to his first tomb the mortal remains of the illustrious founder of the Nupolooniun dynasty. The admiration which I feci, as a soldier, for the exalted genius and exploits of that gieat warrior lias caused me to feel the greater pleasure at the choice which my gracious Sovereign has made of mo for mission," Prince Napoleon replied : þÿ the accomplishment of this honourable " General þÿ 1 receive, in the name of the Emperor, the precious relic which the Queen of England has sent to him. I receive it as a testimony of her desire to efface the poignant, remembrances of St. Helena, as a pledge of the friendship which unites the two Sovereigns, and as a proof of the. alliance which exists between the two nations. May that alliance long continue, for the happiness of the human race ! May it. reserve for the future as great results as those which it has already produced ! 1 am charged by the Emperor to inform you, Genera!, that he particularly appreciates the choice which the Queen lias made of you for this mission. We are happy to have to thank one of those glorious chiefs of the English Army, by the side of whom we have fought, and for whom we have retained such a high esteem." The short ceremonial then terminated. The car is to be placed in the Chapel St. Jerome, by the side of tile mortal remains of the great man which had been conveyed on it to the tomb.

NAPLES. A terrible circumstance h as just occurred in two of the prisons of Naples þÿ those of the Yi caria, and of St. Francesco. The Neapolitan jails are, all under the patronage of the Jesuits, who, being equally detested by turnkeys and prisoners, have found among the latter a ceifain number of disciples who play the part of spies. The inmates of the two prisons by a secret and mysterious understanding, resolved to get rid of those spies at the same hour (6 o'clock, p.m.), on the same day (The 12th of October), to the same rallying word. The plot was duly executed. The conspirators fell upon the spies, and wounded many of them with knives. At the cries which arose the .Swiss, who guard the prisoners, came to the rescue. The disturbance increased. The soldiers fired light and left. The revolt then became general. Danger seeming imminent, the entrance gates were barricaded, and soldiers and turnk ys withdrew. At the dawn of the following day the prisoners were called upon to give up the leaders ol the fray. A horrible night had these prisoners with each other, vengeance everywhere doing its work ; yet, to the summons of the soldier.-, there was a refusal. At this grenades were thrown into the midst of the insurgents hv the Swiss, and the havoc they played, wounding and killing in every direction, compelled the prisoners to yield Tranquillity was thus restored The dead were carried away ; the living were subjected to the punishment of a hundred blows each ; and the most criminal

RUSSIA. The Russian Gazette of St. Petersburg , of the 30th October, gives an account of the election of municipal councillors by the inhabitants of

two villages in the suburbs of St. Petersburg. These inhabitants had been attached to the glebe as serfs of the Admiralty since Peter the Great's time, and were forced to work as carpenters The Emperor Alexander II., by a ukase published in the month of March, this year, enfranchised them, giving them the power of becoming citizens of the capital itself, or of forming a distinct community apart. The number of the persons thus freed amounts to 13.5 of both sexes. The Emperor Alexander has addressed the nobility at Moscow, or rather the nobility of the whole empire, in grave and severe terms, on the apathy they have displayed in reference to the abolition of serfdom. The European Mails for this Island arrived here from St. Thomas this morning. The London Journals are devoid of any news. A perfect calm seems to pervade the political world ; which, however, may be but the harbinger of coming storms.

An accident of a nature which might have resulted in loss of property by fire, took place on Saturday evening in Company Street. An old and infirm lady, Miss Ulrica Bruun, in lighting her candle, accidentally set fire to her cap or some other head-covering, and in the attempt to extinguish it, the flames caught her curtains and extended to other parts of her bed. On the flames' being seen in the street prompt assistance was immediately rendered, in time to prevent the further extension of the fire, but unfortunately too late to save the life of the unfortunate lady, who expired a few hours after from the effects of the severe burns which she received.

Suicide. þÿ On Sunday morning the body of a soldier, named Carl Christian Mortensen Gjerlovmad, was discovered hanging to a tree in the garden of the military barracks in this town. The supposed cause which led to the commission of this fatal act, is reported to be the effect on his mind of some punishment which he lately underwent for disorderly conduct.

FRANCE. The trial of Count do Montalembert, and M. Rouniol, editor of a periodical called the Correspondant, charged with having published a seditious libel, entitled " A Debate on India in the English Parliament," commenced at twelve on Wednesday before the Sixth Chamber of Correctional Police, presided over by M. Berthclin. As early as nine o'clock the doors of the court were besieged by a multitude of persons provided with tickets. The proceedings commenced at twelve o'clock precisely. The pleading lasted till half-past six. The tribunal was one hour considering the verdict. The sitting was resumed at half-past seven. The verdict sentenced M. de Montalembert to six months' imprisonment and 3000f. fine. The editor of tho Correspondant was sentenced to one month's imprisonment and lOOf. fine. The most eloquent orator of France, and one of her most honourable and distinguished children, the Count de Montalembert, has been brought to trial before some police Judges; and, after the farce of their retiring for an hour to consider the sentence, which had been dictated to them a fortnight before by their Imperial master, a statesman and patriot of whom any na tion might be justly proud was sentenced to a fine of three thousand francs and to an imprisonment of six months, for daring to praise English institutions and the English character. It is not worth while to introduce personal considerations into the question. The ingratitude of the French Court towards M. de Montalembert for the support lie rendered to the dynasty he then little understood is natural þÿ almost complimentary to him. The real consideration is the judicial blindness with which despotism is in due season visited. It is impossible that this incarceration of one of the first men in France should not be the harbinger of events perhaps less distant than is supposed by those who, with folded arms, closed lips, and swelling hearts, witness, in silent wrath, the triumph of brute force. Meantime the clash of M. de Moutalembcrt's dungeon doors is drowned in the universal shout of indignation which breaks from all whose voices are free. How the prisoner will be released is scarcely matter for speculation þÿ probably by the efllux of his term of sentence, possibly in a briefer fashion. Lisbon has been visited by an earthquake

þÿ a happily trifling one to be coupled with the name of Lisbon þÿ which recalls the awful event of 1755 ; but still a shock which would have sent any other city of Europe into ecstasies of terror. All the houses are stated to have been shaken for half a minute ; but the wise precautions of Dc Pombal, the Minister of the time when Lisbon was rebuilt, had given to the architecture an elasticity (by means of the till then unknown introduction of woodwork on a large scale, which enabled the houses to stand a strain that would have been fatal to stone. A single life only was lost in the city, but in the suburbs several casualties occurred. Lisbon has not been fortunate in her last two distinguished visitors, France and the earthquake, and it is hard to say which was the last welcome.

MILITARY DEFENCE OF TIIE WEST INDIES. The riots which have recently occurred in Antigua have afforded to our new Colonial Minister au opportunity, whereof he has not been slow to avail himself, of explaining the line of policy Government propose to pursue in regard of Military arrangements in the archipelago of the British Antilles. His despatch to Mr. Hamilton, the intelligent Governor-General of the Leeward Islands, is apparently intended to convey a meaning much larger than that which in terms it expresses þÿ for although in terms Sir Bulwer Lytton expresses only the design of Government to confide to the Islanders alone the means of repressing internal disorders þÿ that design has palpably a far wider scope. The West Indies are to be denuded of Troops, and their inhabitants are, therefore, to provide for their own police; but if denuded of Troops, will not the duty also devolve upon them of providing for their sccurity against external aggression as well as against domestic disturbance ? There can be but one answer to the question. Deprived of Military aid from Imperial resources, or denied it until the danger is closo at hand, the colonists must look to themselves, if either France or the United States should take a fancy to those lovely Islands, which stud tho Western seas Iroin the | embouchure of the Gulf of Florida to tho feverous coasts of Caraccas, and constitute one of the most important Military stations in the whole world. Certain it is that when open war should break

out between Great Britain and either Power, or both, our Fleets would be despatched in all haste, aud Troops as well, to the succour of our West Indian compatriots, whilst the dogged courage, proper to tho British character, and which survives the debilitating influence even of a tropical sun, would induce these to make a desperate and gallant resistance to of the foe. But the bare contemplation such a pos- invading sibility is not agreeable. In their own islands of Martinique and Guadeloupe, aye, and possibly the Spanish islands of Cuba and Porto Ilico, the French would find a point d'appui facilitating their designs in a marvellous way, and giving them besides a most convenient start of us at the commencement of belligerent operations. Toe Admiral of the succouring Fleet may scarcely have hoisted his flag at Portsmouth, before the tricolor -ball be lazily flapping in the evening over the Naval Hospital at Port Royal ; our ships shall be breasting the billows in the hands arc giving tho dockyard at English harbour to the flames ! That the defence of the West Indies from an invader must, in a great measure, be a naval defence may fairly bo conceded þÿ the insular character of these colonies renders this inevitable, but, if all contingencies arc to be provided for, a Military defence is also necessary, and this the colonists have to supply. No one can charge us with a desire to retain any large Forco in the West Indies. It is not requisite to do so, and, in addition, the climate

is unfavorable to the discipline, to the efficiency, to tho very existence of the British Soldier. The lassitude induced by tropical heat leads him to drunkenness and all its attendant evils ; and new rum, to be obtained with such fatal facility, is to him a deadlier enemy even than " Yellow Jack," which he has so much cause to dread. I lures orapula quam gladius is an old saying, but in the West Indies the truth is of a larger range, for there, if pestilence slays his thousands, drink for the support of a Medical man and Dis- | slays his tens of thousands. We have no desire to see more of our Troops broiling and sweltering torrid zone that can possibly be helped; we withdraw from our colonists tho full regis of imperial protection, it would be as well we should ascertain that we do not leave them as their British ancestors were left when tho last Roman Legions evacuated England, with an alterative but, on the one hand, to perish

under the invaders' sword; or, on tho other, to be swallowed up by the angry sea. We have a great respect for Sir Bulwer Lytton, but on this head his despatch is eminently unsatisfactory. It is evident ho relies on a sort of Militia, and, what is a great deal worse, Volunteer Corps as substitutes for the Troops that sooner or later will be abstracted. lie refers to certain local þÿcorps Militia, we presume þÿ which formerly proved of great utility in tho islands, but since have been unwisely sacrificed to economical considerations. To a revival of these, and to the formation of the Corps distinctly volunteer in their character, the Colonial Minister evidently looks as compensating the colonies for the removal of the Regular Troops ; and we only wish we could regard tho matter in the same light. That in every island a Militia should exist, and that every step should be taken to secure its efficiency, wo readily admit. Indeed, as it would be rarely required to act otherwise than ou the defensive we arc to ascribe a large value to the institution of such a Corps; but it. never will, and never can, supply the absence of regularly organized Troops; it never for long could face a Soldiery whom great practice and skilful training had made familiar with all the exigencies ol warfare, aud who had followed leaders, tho business of whose lives had been the direction and handling of large bodies of men. Indeed, a West Indiau Militia, with all the care that may bo bestowed on it, can scarcely be expected to

arrive at that degree of Military proficiency which there is nothing to prevent our Militia Corps at homo from attaining. Our English, Scotch, and Irish Militia Regiments are officered in some degree by Retired Officers of tho Line. It is from tho Lino the Adjutants and Staff Serjeants are invariably, or almost invariably, selected, aud the consequent benefits arc very great. Now, as far as the regimental Officers are concerned, these are advantages our West India Militia can hardly expect to enjoy. The number of Retired Officers settled in the islands must be very small, and contrast strikingly with tho state of things in Canada, especially in Western Canada, in the population of which the Military clement is very influential, and has contributed to niako the provincial Corps ouly inferior to those of the Imperial Army. We have no doubt that when occasion shall arise, tho Militia of Jamaica, of Barbadoes, of Guiana, of Trinidad, will all do their duty to the best of their power; will exhibit all the daring gallantry and loyal devotion we may hope that faithful subjects of tho British crown will always display; but frankly to speak, wo should bo sorry to risk them against tho organised desperadoes of American filibustcrism, and still more against the agile Infantry of France. And if they be found unequal to the encounter, what shall we say of mere Volunteer Corps, who, however they may supplement the exertions of regular Troops can by no possibility afford any substitute for them, and who supply about as

unsatisfactory a means of defence as any we know of. Honestly we confess wc look in a different direction for ensuring th security of the West India Islands. Why not follow the example wc set in Canada, when wo raised the Royal Canadian Riflo Regiment, in St. Helena, in Ceylon, in the Cape, in Malta, antl our settlements on tho Gold Coast ? Why should we not have an addition to our West India Regiments, '"ivging tho coast of maintaiuing the new Battalh ns on the Colonial revenues, and thus furnish a body of really capable Troops officered by men, not mere amateurs, but educated for their calling þÿ Officers, in short, of the Army of the Empire ? The East India Company, before it was reduced as to a caput mor- tuum, bore the whole expense, is well known, of the Queen's Troops furnished lor the defence of its territories. The Government of Victoria towards inoreased allowances to tho Officers and men of the Force there stationed, and we observe that the same boon has been extended to the Officers and cr ' of two men of war lying at Vancouver's I by the providcut care of the local authorii : i that dependency. The West Indians, th, ve would have no reason to complain that tho burden of providing for their defence was devolved upon them, and they would have the less reason to complain if our own proposition were adopted, for then they would have the protection of a Soldiery capable not only -of maintaining internal peace, but of effcotually repelling any aggression that might be attempted,
no matter by whom. þÿ United Service Gazette.

MR. REED IN CHINA. The London Times has obtained what none of our American papers have been able to procure þÿ a copy of the United States treaty with China. On examining it, and with it the evidence of men who have been witnesses of the late diplomatic imbroglio in China, the Times comes to i.ie conclusion that Mr. Reed has sacrificed the interests of the United States to his pique against England, and has concluded a treaty which confers upon American citizens far smaller privileges than they might have obtained had their interests been advocated by a minister of greater skill and clearer mind. The article in the Times is evidently from the pen of Lord Elgin's attache, Mr. Oliphant. Some of our papers have undertaken to deny the statements of the London Times , and to defend Mr. Reed. They have an arduous task before them. The facts tell their own story, and that story is conclusive. Mr. Reed was appointed to the Chinese mission in default of Mr. Walker, who was the man of all others who should have been accredited to Pekin. Mr. Reed was chosen, not from any suspicion of his diplomatic ability (he had never been abroad in any public capacity), but simply because he was an Old-Line Whig, who, during the contest of 1856, had preferred, like most of his brethren, the Buchanan to the Fremont ticket. It was considered only right that those Whigs should be rewarded ; and Mr. Reed was chosen to receive the guerdon on behalf of his sect, lie brought to bear on the mission the experience of a Philadel-

phia lawyer of average reputation. It seems that he no sooner arrived in China than he fell under the influence of Count Putiatin, the Russian envoy. It must be borne in mind by every one that the natural interests of Russia in China are antagonistic to those of the rest of the world. Russia alone of all the nations enjoys regular diplomatic intercourse with Pekin. Russia carries on a large trade with China, which is transacted at Kiakta and other inland entrepots. Russia has no merchant navy to speak of, needs but few Chinese products, and has little to send to China. In all these respects the position of Russia is antagonistic to that of the United States. The United States have no minister at Pekin ; have no inland commercial intercourse with China ; and might, under proper regulations, carry on a large commercial intercourse with the Chinese empire in teas, silks, and Ami rican manufactures. Yet, notwithstanding this palpable diversity of interests between Mr. Reed and Count Putiatin, it seems that the latter is recognized throughout China as the conscience-keeper of the former. The treaty concluded by Mr. Reed between the United States and China is less advantageous than the British and French treaties, inasmuch as it does not provide for a resident American embassy at Pekin, does not secure to United States citizens in China the protection of their own officials, and does not open to the United States people any of the rivers or inland ports of China. Our rivals, the English, have se-

cured all these concessions ; Mr. Reed, who seems to have been led by the nose by his Russian friend, contended for none of them. Mr. Reed left this country at a time when the Russian war had aroused a very remarkable anti-British feeling in the hearts of the American people. Russia was the favorite of the moment þÿ not that we liked her more, but that we hated her less. Mr. Reed seems to have taken this popular whim as the guide of his conduct, and to 1 /e wholly lost sight of the real inte s of the United States in his haste to p .ase Russia

s T.. o 5; a (i x ft v I s , and to spite Great Britain. The result is that we, the ostensible friends of China, have made far worse terms with her than the maritime nations of Europe, which enforced their demands with shot and shell. We never thought much of Mr. Reed as an embassador. A man can no more contend with practical diplomatists, and win diplomatic victories, without apprenticeship, than he can make a boot or a chair ber 1858. without learning the trade. Mr. Reed was a novice, and blundered accordingly. It remains to be seen what will be the fruit of his blunders. If the United States treaty with China is what the London Times represents it to be, it should on no account be ratified by the Senate. Mr. Reed may be suffered to escape with some contempt and derision ; but no treaty between the United States and China should be ratified unless it secure for the United States such advantages as will enable us to contend on other an equal footing with Great Britain for the great Chinese trade þÿ which is destined to be one of the greatest, if not the greatest, commercial movement in the world. þÿ Harper's Weekly Journal
